a2z-0013.intro: A solid block of stars: n rows and n columns forming a perfect square of '*'. It is the simplest pattern of all — the outer loop and the inner work both repeat exactly n times — and it teaches the one idea every pattern in this series is built on: one loop controls the rows, the other controls what each row contains.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Every row is identical: it contains exactly n stars and no leading spaces, so the outer loop simply repeats n times and the inner work for each row is 'print n stars'. If you build the row as a list of n '*' tokens and join them with single spaces, every row comes out as '* * * ... *' with n stars and n-1 gaps between them. There is no per-row formula to vary — the constancy is the point: the row content does not depend on i at all. Total output size is n rows x n stars = n*n stars.

The function builds each row by repeating the '*' token n times in a list and joining with spaces, then prints it. The loop variable i only counts rows — it plays no role in the content. Building the row string first (instead of printing token by token) makes the row-by-row structure visible and avoids stray trailing spaces.

key_points: Outer loop = rows (always n of them); inner work = the contents of one row.
Row content here is independent of the row index i — the same n stars every time.
Joining a token list with ' ' gives clean spacing with no trailing space.
Total stars printed is n * n — this is the 'full grid' every hollow pattern later carves into.
Off-by-one check: range(n) gives exactly n rows, and ['*'] * n gives exactly n stars.

a2z-0014.intro: A flight of stairs made of stars: the first row has 1 star and every row below it has one more, ending with n stars on the last row. This is the archetypal growing triangle — the first pattern where what a row contains depends on which row it is.

sections.body: Number the rows from the top as i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i contains exactly i + 1 stars and no leading spaces — that single formula, stars = i + 1, is the whole pattern. The outer loop walks i from 0 to n-1; for each row you print i + 1 star tokens joined by spaces. The last row (i = n - 1) has n stars, so the triangle's base is exactly as wide as the full n-by-n rectangle of Pattern 1, and the running total of stars is 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2.
For each row index i the code creates a list of i + 1 '*' tokens and prints them joined by spaces. No indent is needed because the triangle is left-aligned — all the growth happens on the right edge.

key_points: Master formula: row i (0-based) prints i + 1 stars.
Left-aligned patterns need no space loop — growth is purely in the token count.
The base row always has exactly n stars; check your last line when debugging.
Using 1-based rows instead? Then row r prints r stars — same thing, just shifted bookkeeping.
This 'count grows with i' idea recurs in Patterns 3, 4, 10, 13, 14 and 16.

a2z-0015.intro: The growing star triangle of Pattern 2 re-skinned with numbers: every row lists the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, ... up to the row's length. It teaches you to generate a row's tokens from a formula on the position inside the row (the column j) instead of repeating one fixed token.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i has i + 1 entries, and the entries are exactly 1, 2, 3, ..., i+1 — so the entry in column j (0-based) of row i is always j + 1, independent of the row. The outer loop fixes the row length (i + 1); the inner loop walks j from 0 to i and emits str(j + 1). The last entry of row i is i + 1, which is also the row's length — a handy self-check while dry-running.

The inner list comprehension builds [str(j + 1) for j in range(i + 1)] — the numbers 1 through i + 1 as strings — and the row is printed joined by spaces. Converting to str before joining is essential: you cannot join integers with a string separator.

key_points: Row i holds i + 1 numbers; the value at column j is j + 1 regardless of the row.
Two loops, two jobs: the outer sets the length, the inner generates values from the column index.
Every row restarts at 1 — the counter is the column, not a running total (contrast Pattern 13).
Convert numbers to strings before ' '.join, or Python raises a TypeError.
Last value of row i equals i + 1 — use it as a quick correctness check.

a2z-0016.intro: A growing triangle where every entry in a row is the same: the row number. Row 1 is just '1', row 2 is '2 2', row 3 is '3 3 3' and so on — Pattern 3 with each row flattened to a single repeated value.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i has i + 1 entries, and every entry equals i + 1 (the 1-based row number). Two facts combine: the count comes from the row index (i + 1 copies) and the value also comes from the row index (the token str(i + 1)). There is no inner variation at all — the inner loop is just a repetition. Compare Pattern 3, where the value came from the column j instead: same skeleton, different source for the token.

The code repeats the single token str(i + 1) exactly i + 1 times in a list and prints it joined by spaces. Because the token never changes within a row, list multiplication [token] * count replaces the inner loop entirely.

key_points: Row i: value = i + 1 and count = i + 1 — both come from the row index.
When a row is one repeated token, list multiplication [tok] * k replaces the inner loop.
Contrast with Pattern 3: there the value came from the column index j + 1.
Watch the +1s: with 0-based rows the printed number is i + 1, not i — row 0 must print '1', never '0'.
The same trick powers Pattern 16 (Alpha-Ramp), with letters instead of digits.

a2z-0017.intro: Pattern 2 flipped upside down: the first row is the full base of n stars and each following row loses one star, until the last row has a single star. It is the fundamental shrinking triangle — the inner count is driven by how many rows remain, not by how many have passed.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i contains exactly n - i stars and no leading spaces. At i = 0 that gives n stars (the full width); at i = n - 1 it gives 1 star. The outer loop still runs n times; only the inner count formula changes, from Pattern 2's i + 1 to n - i. Together, i + 1 and n - i are the two workhorse formulas of this whole series — growing and shrinking.

For each row the code prints a list of n - i '*' tokens joined by spaces. As i climbs, the list shrinks by one each iteration, which is exactly the picture. No indentation is added, so the triangle stays glued to the left margin while its right edge retreats.

key_points: Master formula: row i prints n - i stars — count what is left, not what is done.
First row must be the full n stars; the last row exactly 1.
Growing (i + 1) and shrinking (n - i) counts are the two core formulas of the series.
Left-aligned shrinking needs no spaces; centered shrinking (Pattern 8) adds the space formula.
Total stars printed: n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2.

suggested.note: The same shrinking counts with the numbers 1..n-i instead of stars.

a2z-0018.intro: The numbered counterpart of Pattern 5: the top row lists 1 through n, and each row below drops the largest remaining number, ending with a lone '1'. It drills the shrinking count n - i together with values generated from the column index.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i has n - i entries, and the entries are 1, 2, ..., n-i — so the entry at column j is j + 1, and the row simply stops earlier each time. The outer loop decides the length (n - i); the inner loop fills values from the column (j + 1). Row 0 is the complete sequence 1..n; the final row (i = n - 1) has length 1 and shows just 1.

For each row the code builds [str(j + 1) for j in range(n - i)] — the numbers from 1 up to the current row length — and prints them joined. Changing only the range bound from Pattern 3's i + 1 to n - i converts the growing triangle into this shrinking one.

key_points: Row i: length = n - i and values = 1..(n-i) — both shrink together.
The last number printed in row i equals the row's length — an easy dry-run check.
Patterns 3 and 6 differ by a single bound: i + 1 grows, n - i shrinks.
Values restart at 1 on every row; nothing carries over between rows.
Common slip: using n - i for the count but printing up to n — keep the two in sync.

a2z-0019.intro: A centered pyramid of stars: a single star at the top, and each row below widens by two stars — one stepping left, one stepping right — until the base spans 2n - 1 stars. This is the first pattern that needs two inner ideas at once: leading spaces to center the row, and an odd star count 2i + 1.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i prints n - i - 1 blank slots followed by 2i + 1 stars. The star count is always odd — 1, 3, 5, ... — because the pyramid grows symmetrically around a fixed center column. The blank count shrinks by one per row (n - i - 1), which pulls each row's left edge one slot outward. In this spaced rendering each slot is two characters wide (a token plus its separating space), so the indent is (n - i - 1) pairs of spaces. The base row (i = n - 1) has zero blanks and 2n - 1 stars.

The code computes the indent as '  ' * (n - i - 1) — two spaces per empty slot so the stars line up with the rows below — and joins 2i + 1 '*' tokens for the body, then prints indent + body. Try replacing the double-space indent with a single space and watch the pyramid lean: the alignment lives in that detail.

key_points: Row i: blanks = n - i - 1, stars = 2i + 1 — the two formulas move in opposite directions.
Pyramid widths are the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, ..., 2n - 1.
Each blank slot must be as wide as a printed token (2 chars here), or the centering breaks.
The center column never moves; every row is symmetric around it.
Base check: the last row has 0 leading blanks and exactly 2n - 1 stars.

a2z-0020.intro: The star pyramid of Pattern 7 standing on its head: the first row is the full base of 2n - 1 stars and each row below sheds two stars — one from each side — until a single star remains at the bottom tip. The leading spaces grow exactly as fast as the stars shrink.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i prints i blank slots followed by 2(n - i) - 1 stars. At i = 0: no blanks, 2n - 1 stars. At i = n - 1: n - 1 blanks and exactly 1 star. The star formula 2(n - i) - 1 is just Pattern 7's 2i + 1 run backwards, and the blank count i is Pattern 7's shrinking blank count run forwards. Symmetry around the same center column is preserved on every row.

Each row is '  ' * i for the indent (two characters per empty slot, matching the token width) plus 2(n - i) - 1 joined '*' tokens. The two quantities are computed from the same i, so the rows narrow and drift right in lockstep.

key_points: Row i: blanks = i, stars = 2(n - i) - 1.
Widths step down through the odd numbers: 2n-1, 2n-3, ..., 1.
It is Pattern 7 with both formulas reversed — learn one, derive the other.
The final row is n - 1 blank slots and a single star, sitting on the center column.
Off-by-one trap: 2(n - i) - 1, not 2(n - i) + 1 — test with n = 1, which must print a single star.

a2z-0021.intro: A full diamond: the star pyramid of Pattern 7 stacked directly on top of the inverted pyramid of Pattern 8, giving 2n rows with the widest row of 2n - 1 stars appearing twice in the middle. It shows how the big patterns in this series are assembled from smaller ones you already know.

sections.body: The figure splits into two halves of n rows each. In the top half, row i (0-based within the half) has n - i - 1 blank slots and 2i + 1 stars — exactly Pattern 7. In the bottom half, row i has i blank slots and 2(n - i) - 1 stars — exactly Pattern 8. Because both halves include their widest row, the 2n - 1 star row is printed twice, once as the pyramid's base and once as the inverted pyramid's base. The sequence of widths, 1, 3, ..., 2n-1, 2n-1, ..., 3, 1, is a palindrome, just like the figure.

The code is literally the two earlier solutions pasted together: a first loop running Pattern 7's row formula, then a second loop running Pattern 8's. No new formula is needed — the craft is in reusing the halves verbatim, including the duplicated widest row.

key_points: A diamond = pyramid (Pattern 7) + inverted pyramid (Pattern 8), 2n rows total.
The widest row (2n - 1 stars) appears twice — that duplication is part of the classic shape.
Widths go 1, 3, ..., 2n-1, 2n-1, ..., 3, 1 — palindromic, like the figure itself.
Reuse beats reinvention: if your two halves are correct separately, the diamond is correct.
Variant alert: some versions print the widest row only once (2n - 1 rows) — know which one a problem asks for.

a2z-0022.intro: Half a diamond, sliced vertically: star counts climb 1, 2, 3, ..., n and then descend n-1, ..., 1, all glued to the left edge. With 2n - 1 rows it is the simplest 'go up, then come down' pattern — one count that changes direction at the peak.

sections.body: Number all rows k = 0, 1, ..., 2n - 2 (that is 2n - 1 rows). The star count is k + 1 while k < n (the climb) and 2n - 1 - k once k >= n (the descent). At the peak row k = n - 1 the count is exactly n, and it appears only once — unlike Pattern 9's doubled widest row. Equivalently, the count is min(k + 1, 2n - 1 - k): the distance-driven minimum of the 'growing' and 'shrinking' formulas. There are no leading spaces; the silhouette comes purely from the count.

A single loop runs over all 2n - 1 rows and picks the count with an if/else: i + 1 on the way up, 2n - 1 - i on the way down. One print statement serves both halves — the direction change lives entirely in the count formula.

key_points: Rows = 2n - 1; counts run 1, 2, ..., n, ..., 2, 1 with the peak n printed once.
Count formula: i + 1 while i < n, else 2n - 1 - i — equivalently min(i + 1, 2n - 1 - i).
Contrast Pattern 9: there the widest row repeats; here the peak appears a single time.
No space loop at all — the silhouette comes purely from the count.
Bounds check: range(2n - 1) rows, and the last row must be a single star.

a2z-0023.intro: A growing triangle filled with alternating 0s and 1s. Each row starts with 1 if it is an even row and 0 if it is odd, then flips at every step across the row — a chessboard rule folded into a triangle.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1 and the columns within a row j = 0, 1, ..., i. The entry at (i, j) is 1 when i + j is even and 0 when i + j is odd — equivalently, the entry flips every time you move one step right or one step down. Row i therefore starts with 1 for even i and 0 for odd i, then alternates. You can compute each entry from the parity of i + j, or carry a 'current bit' variable that toggles after every print; both produce the same figure.

The code picks the row's starting bit from the row parity (1 if i is even, else 0) and then generates (start + j) % 2 for each column j — adding j flips the bit back and forth across the row. No state is carried between rows; each row is recomputed from its own indices.

key_points: Entry (i, j) = 1 if i + j is even, else 0 — one parity rule generates the whole figure.
Row i starts with 1 when i is even and 0 when i is odd.
Within a row the bits strictly alternate; a repeated bit means a bug.
Parity thinking (n % 2) is the entire engine — no counters or memory needed.
Edge case n = 1 prints just '1'.

a2z-0024.intro: Two number triangles facing each other across a closing gap: the left side counts up 1, 2, 3, ... while the right side mirrors it back down, and in the last row the two sides meet to form the palindrome 1 2 3 4 4 3 2 1. It is the classic number crown — a lesson in splitting a row into a left part, a gap, and a right part.

sections.body: Use 1-based rows r = 1, 2, ..., n. Row r has three parts: a left run of the numbers 1..r, a middle gap of 2(n - r) empty slots, and a right run of the numbers r..1 in decreasing order. The total slots per row are r + 2(n - r) + r = 2n — constant for every row — which is why all rows have the same printed width. As r grows by 1, each side gains one number and the gap loses two slots, so the sides march toward each other until at r = n the gap vanishes and the row reads 1..n followed by n..1.

The code builds the left list [1..r], a gap list of 2(n - r) single-space placeholders, and the right list [r..1], then joins everything with spaces. Using a blank string as a placeholder token keeps every slot the same width, so the right side stays perfectly aligned as the gap shrinks.
sections.code:
def pattern(n):
    for i in range(n):
        r = i + 1
        left = [str(x) for x in range(1, r + 1)]
        gap = [" "] * (2 * (n - r))
        right = [str(x) for x in range(r, 0, -1)]
        print(" ".join(left + gap + right))

key_points: Row r = left run (1..r) + gap of 2(n - r) slots + right run (r..1).
Every row occupies exactly 2n slots — constant width is the alignment guarantee.
Each step down: the sides grow by 1 each and the gap shrinks by 2.
The final row is a palindrome: 1 2 ... n n ... 2 1.
Placeholder tokens (' ') keep spacing uniform; printing raw spaces inline is where alignment usually breaks.

a2z-0025.intro: Floyd's triangle: a growing number triangle where the counting never restarts. A single counter starts at 1 and keeps incrementing across the entire figure, so rows of length 1, 2, 3, ... consume consecutive numbers and the last entry of the whole triangle is the triangular number n(n+1)/2.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1; row i has i + 1 entries. Keep one variable, num, initialised to 1 before the outer loop. The inner loop appends num to the current row and increments it, i + 1 times per row. Because num lives outside both loops, its value carries across rows — that single scoping decision is the entire difference from Pattern 3, where each row recomputed its values from the column index. Before row i starts, the counter equals 1 + i(i+1)/2, giving the row-start values 1, 2, 4, 7, 11.

The counter num is created once, before the loops. Each row collects i + 1 successive values into a list (incrementing num after each) and prints them joined. Moving the num = 1 line inside the outer loop would reset it every row and reproduce Pattern 3 — scope is the algorithm here.

key_points: One running counter across all rows: never reset it inside the outer loop.
Row i has i + 1 entries; the first entry of row i is 1 + i(i+1)/2.
The final printed number is the triangular number n(n+1)/2 — for n = 5, that is 15.
Variable scope is the whole trick: state created outside the loop persists, state inside resets.
Two-digit numbers (10+) will misalign columns in a naive join — expected in the classic version.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i has i + 1 letters: A, B, C, ..., up to the (i+1)-th letter. The letter at column j is chr(ord('A') + j) — you add the column offset to A's character code and convert back. The row always restarts from A (the value depends on the column, not on any running state), and the last letter of row i is chr(ord('A') + i). For n up to 26 the letters stay inside A-Z; beyond that the classic pattern is not defined.

A list comprehension generates chr(ord('A') + j) for j in range(i + 1) — the letters from A up to the row's last letter — and the row is printed joined by spaces. All the machinery of Pattern 3 carries over; only the token generator changed, from str(j + 1) to a character computation.

key_points: Letter at column j: chr(ord('A') + j) — character arithmetic replaces number formatting.
Row i ends at the (i+1)-th letter and always restarts at A.
Same skeleton as Pattern 3: the outer loop sets the length, the inner generates from the column.
Defined for n <= 26; beyond Z the alphabet runs out.
In C++ or Java the same trick is char('A' + j) — the idea is portable across languages.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i has n - i letters: A, B, ..., up to the (n - i)-th letter. The letter at column j is still chr(ord('A') + j) — values come from the column exactly as in Pattern 14 — but the row length now follows the shrinking formula n - i instead of i + 1. Row 0 is the full run A..(n-th letter); the last row (i = n - 1) has length 1 and prints just A.

The code generates letters for j in range(n - i) and joins them. Only the range bound differs from Pattern 14 — a one-token change that flips the triangle from growing to shrinking, which is precisely the lesson: the shape lives in the bounds.

key_points: Row i: length = n - i, letters A .. chr(ord('A') + n - i - 1).
Values still come from the column index; only the row length formula changed.
First row is the longest (n letters); the last row is the single letter A.
Patterns 14 and 15 together show i + 1 vs n - i driving identical inner logic.
The set of rows is the same as Pattern 14's, printed in reverse order.

a2z-0028.intro: A ramp of letters where each row is one letter repeated: 'A', then 'B B', then 'C C C'. The letter climbs the alphabet as you go down while the repetition count climbs with it — both the value and the count are read off the row index.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i consists of the single letter chr(ord('A') + i) repeated i + 1 times. Nothing depends on the column at all: within a row every token is identical, so the inner loop degenerates to a repetition. This is Pattern 4 (the repeated-number triangle) translated into letters — value from the row index, count = row index + 1.

The code computes the row's letter once, ch = chr(ord('A') + i), builds a list of i + 1 copies with [ch] * (i + 1), and prints it joined. Because the token is constant within the row, list multiplication replaces the inner loop entirely, just as in Pattern 4.

key_points: Row i: letter = chr(ord('A') + i), count = i + 1 — both from the row index alone.
Constant rows are built with [token] * count; no inner loop needed.
This is Pattern 4 with letters — same formulas, character tokens.
Row 0 must be a single 'A'; if you see 'B' first, your offset is wrong.
The right edge forms a staircase while the letters form a ramp — hence the name.

suggested.note: Letters vary by column there; here they vary only by row — a clean contrast.

a2z-0029.intro: A hill of letters, centered like the star pyramid: each row climbs A, B, C, ... up to a peak letter and then descends symmetrically back to A, so every row is a palindrome. Row widths are the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, ..., 2n - 1, matching Pattern 7's skeleton.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i begins with n - i - 1 blank slots (the same centering as Pattern 7), then prints 2i + 1 letters: an ascending run A, B, ..., chr(ord('A') + i) of length i + 1, followed by a descending run of length i that walks back down to A. The peak letter of row i is the (i+1)-th letter, and it appears exactly once, at the center. The bottom row (i = n - 1) climbs to the n-th letter and returns, spanning 2n - 1 letters with no indentation.

The code builds the ascending list [chr(ord('A') + j) for j in range(i + 1)] and the descending list for j from i - 1 down to 0, concatenates them, and prefixes the indent '  ' * (n - i - 1). Splitting the row into an up-run and a down-run makes the palindrome structure explicit and avoids tracking a direction flag inside one loop.

key_points: Row i: blanks = n - i - 1, letters = 2i + 1 (i + 1 ascending, then i descending).
The peak letter chr(ord('A') + i) appears once, exactly at the center.
Every row is a palindrome — read it backwards to check your descending run.
Same centering math as Pattern 7; only the token generator changed.
Common bug: starting the descent at the peak itself (duplicating it) — start at i - 1 instead.

a2z-0030.intro: A letter triangle where each row slides one step earlier in the alphabet: the top row is the single last letter (E for n = 5), and every row below starts one letter sooner and runs up to that same final letter, ending with the full run A B C D E. It is a growing triangle whose starting value — not just its length — moves with the row.

sections.body: Number the rows i = 0, 1, ..., n-1. Row i has i + 1 letters, ending at the n-th letter chr(ord('A') + n - 1) and starting at chr(ord('A') + n - 1 - i). So the start letter walks backwards down the alphabet as i grows: for n = 5 the rows start at E, D, C, B, A. Within a row the letters simply ascend by one from the start. Two quantities move together — length = i + 1 and start offset = n - 1 - i — and their sum is always n - 1, which is why every row ends at the same final letter.

The code computes the row's starting character code, start = ord('A') + n - 1 - i, then generates i + 1 consecutive letters from it. All rows share the same right edge (the n-th letter); only the left edge moves — that is the whole design.

key_points: Row i: start = chr(ord('A') + n - 1 - i), length = i + 1, and the end is always the n-th letter.
Start offset and length sum to n - 1 on every row — the invariant that keeps the right edge fixed.
Unlike Pattern 14, rows do not restart at A; each starts one letter earlier than the row above.
Read the figure diagonally: each descending diagonal is a constant letter.
The top row is a single letter — the n-th one, not A. Getting E (for n = 5) confirms the offset math.

suggested.title: Pattern 15 — Reverse Letter Triangle Pattern
suggested.note: Letters shrink from a fixed start at A; here they grow toward a fixed end.

suggested.note: The basic letter triangle — every row restarts at A there.

a2z-0031.intro: Two solid blocks of stars separated by a void that opens and then closes: the figure starts as one solid band of 2n stars, splits into two blocks that drift apart until only single stars remain at the edges, then comes back together. It is Pattern 12's 'two sides plus a gap' idea rendered in stars and mirrored top-to-bottom.

sections.body: Think of each row as three parts across a fixed canvas of 2n slots: a left block of stars, a gap of blank slots, and a right block equal to the left. In the top half, row i (0-based) has n - i stars per side and a gap of 2i slots — the void widens by two each row as the blocks erode from the inside. The bottom half runs the same formulas in reverse: row i has i + 1 stars per side and a gap of 2(n - i - 1) slots. The middle two rows are identical (1 star, a gap of 2n - 2 slots, 1 star), and the first and last rows are the solid 2n-star band.

The code builds rows as token lists — side stars, then gap placeholders (' ' tokens that keep slot widths uniform), then side stars again — and joins them. A first loop generates the opening half and a second loop the closing half; concatenating the two lists and printing them in order gives the full symmetric figure.

key_points: Row anatomy: side stars + gap + side stars, always totalling 2n slots.
Top half row i: stars per side = n - i, gap = 2i. The bottom half mirrors it.
The two middle rows are identical — the void is widest there (2n - 2 slots).
Placeholder blank tokens keep both blocks aligned; raw space printing breaks the right block.
The figure is symmetric both horizontally and vertically — fold it either way to check.

suggested.title: Pattern 20 — Symmetry Pattern
suggested.note: The inverse journey: blocks start separated and grow toward each other.

suggested.title: Pattern 12 — Number Crown Pattern
suggested.note: The same left + gap + right construction with numbers.

suggested.title: Pattern 21 — Hollow Rectangle Pattern
suggested.note: Another figure defined by its border and a hollow interior.

suggested.title: Reverse an array
suggested.note: Mirrored halves meeting in the middle — the same symmetry, in array form.

a2z-0032.intro: The mirror journey of Pattern 19: two star triangles start as far apart as possible — single stars at the far edges — and grow toward each other row by row until they merge into a solid band of 2n stars at the center, then separate again. The figure is symmetric across both axes, like an hourglass turned on its side.

sections.body: Use a single row counter k = 0, 1, ..., 2n - 1 (2n rows). Let s = min(k, 2n - 1 - k) + 1 — the distance from the nearer end, plus one. Row k has s stars on the left, a gap of 2(n - s) blank slots, and s stars on the right, always filling the same 2n-slot canvas. At the ends (k = 0 and k = 2n - 1) s = 1: lone stars at the edges with the maximum void of 2n - 2 slots. In the middle (k = n - 1 and k = n) s = n: the gap closes completely and the row is solid. The min() folds the second half onto the first, so one formula generates the whole figure.

One loop over 2n rows computes side_count from the folded index min(k, 2n - 1 - k) + 1, then joins side stars, gap placeholders, and side stars. Folding the index with min() is the key move — it makes the bottom half automatically mirror the top without a second loop.

key_points: Row k: side = min(k, 2n - 1 - k) + 1 stars, gap = 2(n - side) slots — one formula, whole figure.
2n rows; the solid 2n-star row appears twice at the center.
Index folding with min() replaces a second, mirrored loop.
It is Pattern 19 run backwards: the void closes, then reopens.
Every row spans exactly 2n slots — check the first and last rows for equal width.

suggested.title: Pattern 19 — Symmetric-Void Pattern
suggested.note: The same canvas with the motion reversed — the void opens first, then closes.

suggested.note: Another fully symmetric figure assembled from mirrored halves.

suggested.title: Pattern 10 — Half Diamond Star Pattern

a2z-0033.intro: A hollow square: stars form only the border of an n-by-n frame while the interior stays empty. It turns Pattern 1's solid block inside out — instead of asking 'how many stars per row?', you ask 'is this cell on the boundary?'

sections.body: Consider the n-by-n grid of cells (i, j) with rows and columns 0-based. A cell gets a star exactly when it lies on the border: i = 0 (top row), i = n - 1 (bottom row), j = 0 (left column), or j = n - 1 (right column). Interior cells (0 < i < n - 1 and 0 < j < n - 1) are blank slots. So the first and last rows are solid n-star lines, and every middle row is a star, then n - 2 blank slots, then a star. The boundary-condition test — not a count — is the idea to take away; it generalises to hollow triangles, hollow diamonds, and grids of any shape.

The code special-cases the first and last rows as solid lines, and for middle rows joins a star, n - 2 blank placeholder tokens, and a star. An equivalent version loops over every cell and prints a star exactly when the border condition holds — it exposes the rule directly and extends to other shapes.

key_points: Star rule: print '*' exactly when i == 0 or i == n - 1 or j == 0 or j == n - 1.
Middle rows are always: 1 star, n - 2 blanks, 1 star.
Total stars = 4n - 4 (the perimeter) versus n*n for the solid Pattern 1.
Placeholder blanks keep the right border aligned with the solid rows.
Edge cases: n = 1 prints one star; n = 2 prints a solid 2x2 (no interior exists).

suggested.title: Pattern 1 — Rectangular Star Pattern
suggested.note: The solid block this frame is carved from — compare star counts n*n vs 4n - 4.

suggested.title: Pattern 19 — Symmetric-Void Pattern
suggested.note: Another figure whose identity is a border plus a managed void.

suggested.title: Pattern 22 — Number Pattern
suggested.note: Cells classified by distance to the border — the natural next step from boundary tests.

suggested.title: Sum of Array Elements
suggested.note: Full-grid traversal; this pattern is what happens when the traversal gains a condition.

a2z-0034.intro: A square of numbers arranged in concentric layers like an onion: the outermost ring is all n, the next ring in is n - 1, and the value drops by one per layer until the single center cell holds 1. For n = 4 the square is 7x7, and the figure reads identically along every row, column, and line of symmetry.

sections.body: The grid has size 2n - 1 (so there is a single center cell). For the cell at (i, j), compute its distance to the nearest edge: dist = min(i, j, size - 1 - i, size - 1 - j). Edge cells have dist 0, the next ring dist 1, and the center dist n - 1. The printed value is n - dist. That is the whole pattern — no row or column formula, just 'how deep is this cell?'. Every ring of constant dist is a square frame of the kind Pattern 21 draws, and the frames nest inside each other.

Two nested loops walk the (2n - 1) x (2n - 1) grid. For each cell the code takes the minimum of the four distances to the edges and prints n minus that distance. The min-of-four-distances idiom is the entire algorithm — everything else is the standard grid-printing skeleton from Pattern 1.

key_points: Grid size is 2n - 1, not n — the input counts layers, and layers need a center.
Cell value = n - min(i, j, size-1-i, size-1-j): distance to the nearest edge decides everything.
Each constant-value ring is a hollow square — Pattern 21 nested inside itself.
The center cell is always 1 and the border is always n — instant sanity checks.
The figure has four-way symmetry: rows read the same as columns.

suggested.note: One hollow frame; this pattern nests that frame inside itself n times.

a2z-0123.intro: Hashing is the technique of turning a value into a direct memory address so it can be found in (average) constant time. In this module you use it in its most powerful competitive-programming form: not just counting frequencies, but combining a hash map with prefix sums to answer questions about subarrays — longest subarray with a given sum, how many subarrays have a given sum or XOR — in one linear pass.

sections.h: What a hash map actually does
sections.body:
A hash map stores key-value pairs. When you insert a key, a hash function converts it into a bucket index, and the pair is stored in that bucket. Looking the key up later means hashing it again and jumping straight to the same bucket, so insert, lookup and delete are O(1) on average.

Collisions — two different keys landing in the same bucket — are handled by chaining (each bucket holds a small list of pairs) or open addressing. As the table fills up, a load factor threshold triggers a resize and rehash so buckets stay short. You rarely implement this yourself: Python's dict and set, C++'s unordered_map and Java's HashMap are all hash maps. What you must internalise is the cost model: average O(1) per operation, worst case O(n) if many keys collide, and O(n) extra space.

The simplest hashing pattern is counting how often each value occurs. One pass builds the frequency map; after that, questions like 'does any element appear twice?', 'is this a valid anagram?' or 'what is the majority element?' become quick lookups instead of nested loops.

A close cousin is the 'have I seen this before?' set. While scanning left to right, a set of seen values lets you detect duplicates, find the first repeated element, or check membership in O(1) per step. Whenever a brute-force solution has an inner loop that only searches for a value, a hash set or map usually deletes that loop.

sections.h: Prefix sums + hashing: the subarray trick
sections.body:
Let prefix[i] be the sum of the first i elements. The sum of the subarray (j+1 .. i) is prefix[i] - prefix[j]. So a subarray ending at i has sum K exactly when some earlier prefix equals prefix[i] - K.

While scanning, keep a hash map of prefixes you have already seen. At each step compute the running prefix P, then ask the map: have I seen P - K? If yes, a subarray ending here sums to K. For the LONGEST such subarray, store only the first (earliest) index of each prefix. For COUNTING subarrays, store how many times each prefix occurred and add that count to the answer.

The one detail everyone forgets: seed the map with prefix 0 before the scan starts (index -1 for the longest version, count 1 for the counting version). That represents the empty prefix before the array begins, and without it, subarrays starting at index 0 are missed.
sections.code:
def longest_subarray_with_sum(arr, k):
    first_seen = {0: -1}        # prefix sum -> earliest index
    prefix = 0
    best = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(arr):
        prefix += x
        if prefix - k in first_seen:
            best = max(best, i - first_seen[prefix - k])
        if prefix not in first_seen:   # keep earliest only
            first_seen[prefix] = i
    return best

sections.h: Worked example: longest subarray with sum 3
sections.body:
Take arr = [1, -1, 5, -2, 3] and K = 3. Running prefixes (with the seeded 0 at index -1) are: 0, 1, 0, 5, 3, 6.

At the last element the prefix is 6, and 6 - 3 = 3 was first seen at index 3, giving length 5 - 3 = 2... but the better hit comes earlier: when the prefix is 3 (after the fourth element, index 3), 3 - 3 = 0 matches the seeded prefix at index -1, giving length 3 - (-1) = 4. That is the subarray [1, -1, 5, -2], which indeed sums to 3, and it is the longest.

Notice why this module needs hashing at all: the array contains negatives, so prefix sums go up and down. Sliding window relies on sums moving in one direction only, so it cannot be used here — the hash map version works for any integers.

The prefix + hash approach is O(n) average time and O(n) space, against O(n^2) for checking all subarrays. The same skeleton solves the XOR variant (prefix XOR instead of prefix sum, using the fact that x XOR x = 0) and 'largest subarray with sum 0' (K = 0).

Common mistakes: (1) overwriting the stored index of a prefix — for longest problems you must keep the earliest occurrence, for counting you must accumulate counts, and mixing the two recipes gives wrong answers; (2) forgetting the seeded prefix 0; (3) reaching for a hash map when order matters — hash maps do not remember insertion order of keys for range questions, and they cannot answer 'smallest value greater than x' (that needs a balanced BST / sorted structure); (4) in languages like C++, using unordered_map with hackable hash functions can be forced into worst-case collisions, so competitive programmers often use gp_hash_table or sort + coordinate compression instead.

key_points: Hash maps give average O(1) insert, lookup and delete; worst case degrades to O(n) under heavy collisions.
Subarray sum K exists ending at i iff an earlier prefix equals prefix[i] - K — store prefixes in a hash map.
Always seed the map with prefix 0 (earliest index -1, or count 1) so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.
For LONGEST subarray keep the first occurrence of each prefix; for COUNTING keep occurrence counts — never mix the two.
Negative numbers kill sliding window but not prefix + hashing; the XOR version uses prefix XOR instead of prefix sum.

a2z-0173.intro: Almost every recursion problem in this module — subsets, combination sums, subsequences with sum K — is built on one pattern: at each element you branch into 'pick it' or 'skip it'. This lesson pins down the vocabulary (subsequence vs substring vs subset) and that pick / not-pick recursion pattern, including how to attach conditions like a target sum and how to reason about its 2^n cost.

sections.body:
Given a sequence, a subsequence keeps some elements in their original relative order, possibly skipping others. A substring is stricter: the elements must be contiguous. A subset ignores order entirely — it is just a set of chosen elements.

For [1, 2, 3]: subsequences include [1, 3], [2], [1, 2, 3] and the empty sequence — 8 in total. Substrings (contiguous) are only [1], [2], [3], [1, 2], [2, 3], [1, 2, 3] — 6. For an array of n elements there are exactly 2^n subsequences (each element is independently in or out), but only n(n+1)/2 substrings/subarrays. That 2^n is why subsequence problems are exponential by nature and why n is usually small (or why DP enters the picture later).

Write a recursive function f(index, current) that decides the fate of elements from index to the end. At each call you branch twice: once taking arr[index] into current, once leaving it out. When index reaches n, current is one complete subsequence — record it.

The recursion tree has two children per node and depth n, so it has 2^n leaves — one per subsequence. Discipline matters: append the element, recurse, then pop it (backtracking), so a single shared list is reused instead of copying lists at every call.
sections.code:
def subsequences(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    result = []
    current = []

    def dfs(i):
        if i == n:
            result.append(list(current))
            return
        current.append(arr[i])   # pick arr[i]
        dfs(i + 1)
        current.pop()            # undo, then skip arr[i]
        dfs(i + 1)

    dfs(0)
    return result

sections.body:
Most problems add a filter. Three standard variants appear in this module:

Existence — 'is there a subsequence with sum K?' Carry the running sum as a parameter. The moment sum == K at a leaf, return True and let it propagate up immediately; the early exit prunes the rest of the tree, so the best case is far below 2^n.

Counting — 'how many subsequences sum to K?' Return 1 at a successful leaf and 0 otherwise; each internal node returns left + right. No early exit is possible because every branch contributes.

Printing one — keep a flag or return the found subsequence up the chain instead of collecting all of them.

Passing the sum (or remaining target) down as a parameter, instead of recomputing it from current each time, keeps each call O(1).

If the array has duplicate values, plain pick / not-pick generates duplicate subsets. The standard fix for subset-style problems: sort the array first, and at each level skip a value if the same value was just skipped at that level (the 'skip duplicates in the not-pick branch' rule used in Subsets II and Combination Sum II).

Pruning cuts work when the condition allows it: if all numbers are positive and the running sum already exceeds K, the pick branch can be abandoned. With negatives present, no such prune is valid — a later negative could bring the sum back down. Recognising which prunes are legal for the given constraints is the difference between a solution that passes and one that times out.

Generating all subsequences costs O(2^n * n) time (2^n leaves, up to n work to copy each result) and O(n) recursion depth. Counting variants are O(2^n) time. This is only feasible for n up to roughly 20-25; beyond that, the problem is secretly a DP problem (subset-sum DP) or needs meet-in-the-middle.

Common mistakes: forgetting the empty subsequence is a valid leaf result; mutating a shared list without popping after the pick branch, which corrupts sibling branches; recomputing the sum of current at every node (O(n) per node) instead of passing it as a parameter; and, in duplicate problems, deduplicating with a set of tuples at the end — it works but explodes memory compared with the sort-and-skip rule.

key_points: A subsequence preserves order but may skip elements; an array of size n has exactly 2^n subsequences, including the empty one.
Pick / not-pick recursion: branch on taking arr[index] or skipping it, append-pop to reuse one list.
Existence problems can early-exit on the first success; counting problems must explore the whole tree and sum left + right.
Duplicates are handled by sorting first and skipping equal values in the skip branch at each level.
Cost is O(2^n) leaves — fine for n <= ~22; larger n signals DP or meet-in-the-middle instead.

a2z-0190.intro: A linked list stores data in nodes scattered across memory, chained together by pointers, instead of in one contiguous block like an array. This representation trades instant random access for cheap insertions and deletions anywhere in the chain. Almost every linked-list problem in this module reduces to a small set of pointer moves, so this lesson builds the mental model first: what a node is, what head means, and how to walk the list without losing it.

sections.body:
Arrays have two structural annoyances: their size is fixed at creation (or costly to grow), and inserting or deleting in the middle means shifting every element after that point — O(n) data movement. A linked list pays for neither: nodes are allocated one at a time wherever memory is free, and inserting or deleting is just rewiring a couple of pointers.

The price is access. An array gives you arr[i] in O(1) because elements sit at predictable offsets. A linked list has no offsets — to reach the 50th node you must follow 50 next pointers, so access and search are O(n). Keep this trade-off in mind; it explains every complexity figure in this module.

Each node holds two things: the data value, and next — a reference to the following node, or None if this is the last node. The list itself is represented by a single reference, head, pointing at the first node. An empty list is simply head = None. The last node (whose next is None) is called the tail.

Crucially, the chain is the only path through the data. If you ever overwrite a next pointer before saving where it pointed, everything after it becomes unreachable — 'losing the list' is the classic linked-list bug, and most techniques in this module exist to avoid it.

sections.h: Traversal: walking without losing the list
sections.body:
Every read operation — printing, counting length, searching for a value — is the same walk: start a temporary pointer at head, use it, then advance temp = temp.next until temp is None.

Always walk with a separate temp pointer, never with head itself. If you advance head, you have thrown away the start of the list and can never get back. Length counting and linear search are simply this walk with a counter or a comparison added, both O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

Access by position: O(n). Search: O(n). Insert/delete at the head: O(1). Insert/delete at the tail or at position k: O(n) because you must walk there first (the rewiring itself is O(1)). Space per node is O(1) extra for the pointer.

Common mistakes: (1) moving head during traversal instead of a temp pointer; (2) forgetting the empty-list case — almost every operation must ask 'what if head is None?' first; (3) writing temp.next.next without checking temp.next exists, which crashes on the last node; (4) assuming a tail pointer exists — a plain singly linked list keeps only head unless you maintain a tail reference yourself, as array_to_list above does temporarily during construction.

key_points: A node = data + next pointer; the list is just the head reference, and the last node's next is None.
Arrays win on random access O(1); linked lists win on insert/delete at a known position O(1) rewiring.
Never traverse with head itself — use a temp pointer or you lose the list.
Reaching any position costs O(n); only work at the head is truly O(1).
Every operation must first handle head = None (empty list).

a2z-0192.intro: Deleting a node from a singly linked list is pure pointer surgery: you never 'remove' memory directly, you just make the chain skip over the unwanted node, and the language's garbage collector reclaims it. This lesson walks through the four standard deletion cases — head, tail, position k, and a given value — because every harder deletion problem in this module is one of these cases in disguise.

sections.h: The core idea: deletion is rewiring
sections.body:
To delete a node X, the node before X must point to the node after X. That single observation drives everything. It also explains the singly linked list's central awkwardness: given only a node, you cannot find its predecessor — you must walk from head keeping track of the previous node as you go.

Two things must be returned or preserved in every deletion routine: the (possibly new) head, and correctness on edge cases — empty list, single-node list, and deleting the first or last element. Handle those first in code, and the general case becomes short.

The easiest case. If the list is empty, there is nothing to do — return None. Otherwise the new head is simply head.next; the old head becomes unreachable. This is O(1).

Forgetting to return the new head is the classic bug here: the deletion 'worked' inside the function, but the caller still points at the deleted node.

The tail has no successor, so deletion means making the second-last node the new tail: walk until temp.next.next is None — temp is then the second-last node — and set temp.next = None.

Edge cases: empty list returns None; a single-node list returns None too (deleting its tail deletes everything). The walk makes this O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.h: Case 3: deleting the k-th node, and Case 4: deleting by value
sections.body:
For position k (1-indexed): if k == 1, it is the head case. Otherwise walk to the node just before position k, keeping a prev pointer, then splice: prev.next = prev.next.next. Guard against k being larger than the length — if you run off the end, leave the list unchanged.

Deleting by value X is the same shape: walk with prev and temp; when temp.data == X, splice prev.next = temp.next and stop. If X is in the head node, it degenerates to the head case again. Both are O(n) time and O(1) space.

(1) Not returning the head — deletion of the first node changes what head is, so every delete function must return head and callers must use it. (2) Splicing with temp.next = temp.next.next without first confirming temp.next is not None. (3) In the by-value case, stopping the search at the tail without checking whether the tail itself holds X — the loop condition above checks prev.next, so the tail is examined too; get the condition shape right. (4) In C/C++, forgetting to free/delete the removed node leaks memory; in Python and Java the garbage collector handles it once the node is unreferenced.

key_points: Deletion = make the predecessor point past the deleted node; the node itself is never modified.
Deleting the head is O(1) and changes head — the function must return the new head.
Tail, k-th and by-value deletions all walk with a prev pointer: O(n) time, O(1) space.
Always handle empty list and single-node list before the general case.
In a singly linked list you cannot delete a node given only that node (without its value trick) — you need the predecessor.

a2z-0193.intro: Insertion is the mirror image of deletion: create a node, then wire it into the chain in the right order so nothing after the insertion point is lost. This lesson covers the four standard cases — at the head, at the tail, at position k, and before a given value — and the one ordering rule that prevents the most common linked-list bug.

sections.h: The golden rule of insertion order
sections.body:
When splicing a new node between A and B, always point the new node at B first, and only then point A at the new node.

If you rewire A first (A.next = new_node) before saving B, the reference to B — and the entire rest of the list — is gone. Every insertion case below is just: find the splice point, then apply 'new node points forward first, predecessor points at new node second'.

sections.h: Case 1: insert at head, Case 2: insert at tail
sections.body:
At the head: the new node's next is the old head, and the new node becomes head. O(1), and it works on an empty list with no special casing (old head is None, which is exactly the right next).

At the tail: if the list is empty, the new node is the head. Otherwise walk to the last node (temp.next is None) and attach the new node there. O(n) for the walk.

Positions are 1-indexed: inserting at position k means the new node becomes the k-th node, and the node previously at k shifts to k+1, so you splice after the (k-1)-th node. If k == 1, it is the head case. If k is beyond length+1, most problem statements treat it as invalid or as an append — read the statement.

Walk with a counter to position k-1, then apply the golden rule: new_node.next = temp.next; temp.next = new_node.
sections.code:
def insert_at_k(head, x, k):
    new_node = Node(x)
    if k == 1:
        new_node.next = head
        return new_node
    temp = head
    count = 1
    while temp is not None and count < k - 1:
        temp = temp.next
        count += 1
    if temp is None:              # k out of range
        return head
    new_node.next = temp.next     # 1) point forward first
    temp.next = new_node          # 2) then link predecessor
    return head

sections.h: Case 4: insert before a value X
sections.body:
Walk until you find the node whose next holds X — you must stop one node early, because the splice happens at the predecessor. If X is the head's value, it is the head case. If X is absent, the list is left unchanged.

All four insertion cases are O(n) worst case (except head insertion, O(1)) and O(1) extra space besides the new node itself.

(1) Rewiring the predecessor before setting the new node's next — the golden-rule violation that loses the tail of the list. (2) Off-by-one on position k: remember you stop at k-1 because the new node takes position k. (3) Forgetting the empty-list and head-value special cases in the tail and before-value routines. (4) Not returning head from every insert function — inserting at the head changes head just like deleting it did.

key_points: Golden rule: set the new node's next first, then link the predecessor to it — never the other way round.
Insert at head is O(1); tail, position-k and before-value insertions walk first, so O(n).
Position k insertion splices after node k-1; k == 1 is the head case.
Before-value insertion must stop at the predecessor of the target node.
Every insert routine returns the (possibly new) head.

a2z-0204.intro: A doubly linked list gives every node two pointers — next and prev — so the chain can be walked in both directions. That one extra pointer removes the singly linked list's biggest weakness: with a node in hand you can now reach its predecessor in O(1), which makes deletions of a given node constant-time and enables backward traversal. The cost is one extra pointer per node and double the link bookkeeping on every update.

sections.h: Anatomy: node with prev and next
sections.body:
A doubly linked node stores data, next (successor or None at the tail) and prev (predecessor or None at the head). The list is still referenced by head; the head's prev is always None and the tail's next is always None — those two facts are your boundary checks everywhere.

The invariant to protect at all times: for every adjacent pair A -> B, B.prev is A. Any operation that updates a next pointer but forgets the mirror prev pointer leaves the list silently corrupted — forward traversal looks fine while backward traversal breaks. Most DLL bugs are exactly this.

Forward traversal is identical to the singly case: temp from head, follow next. Backward traversal needs the tail first: walk forward to the end once, then follow prev back to the head. Reversing a DLL (a practice problem in this module) exploits exactly this symmetry — swap prev and next on every node, and the old tail becomes the new head.

Because you can move both ways, some problems get cheaper: finding pairs with a given sum in a sorted DLL uses two pointers starting at head and tail moving toward each other, an O(n) trick impossible in a singly list without extra space.

sections.h: What the extra pointer buys — and costs
sections.body:
Buys: (1) delete a node given only that node in O(1) — its neighbours are reachable through prev and next; (2) insert before a given node in O(1); (3) backward traversal and reverse-order processing; (4) cheaper tail deletion, since the tail's predecessor is tail.prev.

Costs: one extra reference per node (memory), and every splice must update up to four links instead of two, with the mirror-image bug risk described above. Insertion and deletion at a known position are still O(1) rewiring, but reaching position k is O(n) just as before.

(1) Updating next but not prev (or vice versa) during a splice — always change links in matched pairs. (2) Forgetting head.prev must be set to None when a new head is created or the old head is deleted. (3) In array_to_dll-style construction, creating the node but forgetting to pass prev=tail, which produces a list that only looks doubly linked. (4) Assuming a stored tail pointer exists — unless you maintain one, reaching the tail still costs a full walk.

key_points: DLL node = data + prev + next; head.prev is None and tail.next is None, always.
Invariant: if B follows A, then B.prev is A — update links in mirror pairs or the list corrupts silently.
Given a node, its predecessor is O(1) away, so delete/insert around a known node is O(1).
Backward traversal and sorted-DLL two-pointer tricks are the practical payoffs.
Cost: one extra pointer per node and roughly double the bookkeeping per update.

a2z-0205.intro: Deleting from a doubly linked list follows the same skip-over idea as the singly case, but every deletion must repair links in both directions: the predecessor's next and the successor's prev. This lesson covers deleting the head, the tail, the k-th node and a given node, with the invariant checks that keep the backward chain intact.

sections.body:
To remove node X with predecessor P and successor N: set P.next = N and N.prev = P. Either link may be absent — if X is the head, there is no P, and the answer is a new head whose prev must be None; if X is the tail, there is no N. If X is the only node, the list becomes empty.

Write the boundary cases first (empty list, single node), then the general splice handles everything else uniformly.

sections.h: Case 1: delete head and Case 2: delete tail
sections.body:
Head: if head is None return None; if head.next is None return None (single node). Otherwise new_head = head.next and new_head.prev = None — forgetting that prev reset is the number-one DLL bug, because the new head still points back at the deleted node.

Tail: walk to the tail (or use tail.prev if you already hold the tail), then tail.prev.next = None. Unlike the singly list, no second-last hunt is needed once you are at the tail — prev gives it to you in O(1).

Walk a temp pointer to position k with a counter. If k == 1 it is the head case; if temp.next is None it is the tail case; in the middle, splice both directions: temp.prev.next = temp.next and temp.next.prev = temp.prev. Because the node carries its own prev, you do not need the separate prev-tracking variable the singly version required — the node knows its predecessor.
sections.code:
def delete_kth_dll(head, k):
    if head is None:
        return None
    temp = head
    count = 1
    while temp is not None and count < k:
        temp = temp.next
        count += 1
    if temp is None:              # k out of range
        return head
    prev_node, next_node = temp.prev, temp.next
    if prev_node is None and next_node is None:
        return None               # only node
    if prev_node is None:
        next_node.prev = None
        return next_node          # new head
    if next_node is None:
        prev_node.next = None
        return head               # new tail
    prev_node.next = next_node
    next_node.prev = prev_node
    return head

sections.h: Case 4: delete a given node (not the head)
sections.body:
Some problems hand you the node itself and promise it is not the head. Then deletion is pure O(1): prev_node.next = node.next, and if node.next exists, node.next.prev = prev_node. No walk at all — this is the payoff for the extra pointer.

Complexity for the other cases is dominated by the walk: O(n) time, O(1) space. Common mistakes: resetting the wrong prev after head deletion; in the k-th case, treating 'k == length' with the middle splice (its next_node is None and next_node.prev would crash — the boundary branches above exist precisely for this); and leaving the deleted node's own pointers dangling into the list, which matters in C++ where you also free the node.

key_points: Every DLL deletion repairs two links: predecessor's next and successor's prev.
After deleting the head, set the new head's prev to None — the most common DLL bug is skipping this.
Deleting the tail or a given node is O(1) once the node is in hand, thanks to prev.
Delete-kth unifies the others: walk, then branch on whether prev/next are None.
Boundary cases first: empty list and single-node list both delete to None.

a2z-0206.intro: Inserting into a doubly linked list means creating a node and wiring four links consistently: the new node's prev and next, plus one link on each neighbour. This lesson covers insertion before the head, before the tail, before the k-th node and before a given node — the four forms the practice problems take — and the update order that keeps both directions valid at every step.

sections.body:
Splicing a new node N between P (predecessor) and S (successor) requires: N.prev = P, N.next = S, P.next = N, S.prev = N. Links touching the new node can be set in any order since N is not yet reachable, but the two neighbour links (P.next and S.prev) should be set after N's own links are ready, and neither neighbour link may be skipped.

Most DLL problems phrase insertion as 'before X' rather than 'after X' — natural for a doubly list because the node you are given can reach its predecessor through prev.

sections.h: Case 1: insert before head, Case 2: insert before tail
sections.body:
Before head: N.next = head, N.prev = None, head.prev = N, and N becomes the new head. This also handles the empty list (head is None, so just return N).

Before tail: walk to the tail T. Its predecessor is T.prev. Splice N between T.prev and T with the four-link rule. If the list has one node, the tail is the head and this degenerates to Case 1.

sections.h: Case 3: insert before the k-th node, Case 4: insert before a given node
sections.body:
Before the k-th node (1-indexed): if k == 1 use the head routine. Otherwise walk to the k-th node T and splice before it using T.prev — identical mechanics to Case 2 with a different target. If k exceeds the length, the target does not exist; leave the list unchanged (or append, per the problem statement).

Before a given node: you are handed T directly, so no walk — read P = T.prev and apply the four-link rule; if P is None, T was the head and the new node becomes head.
sections.code:
def insert_before_kth(head, x, k):
    if k == 1 or head is None:
        return insert_before_head(head, x)
    temp = head
    count = 1
    while temp is not None and count < k:
        temp = temp.next
        count += 1
    if temp is None:              # k out of range
        return head
    prev_node = temp.prev
    node = DNode(x, prev=prev_node, next=temp)
    prev_node.next = node
    temp.prev = node
    return head

def insert_before_node(node, x):
    # returns the (possibly new) head; node must not be None
    prev_node = node.prev
    new_node = DNode(x, prev=prev_node, next=node)
    node.prev = new_node
    if prev_node is None:
        return new_node           # inserted before the old head
    prev_node.next = new_node
    return None                   # head unchanged; caller keeps old head

sections.body:
Rewiring is O(1) in all cases; total cost is O(n) when a walk is needed (tail, k-th) and O(1) for before-head and before-given-node. Space is O(1) beyond the new node.

Common mistakes: (1) setting only three of the four links — usually the successor's prev — so backward traversal skips or resurrects nodes; (2) in before-head insertion, forgetting head.prev = node; (3) in the k-th case, splicing after the k-th node instead of before it (read the problem statement twice — 'insert at position k' and 'insert before the k-th node' differ by one); (4) losing the new head: before-head insertion changes head, so the function must return it and callers must keep it.

key_points: A DLL splice touches four links: new node's prev/next and one link on each neighbour.
Insert before head is O(1) and produces a new head with prev = None.
Before-tail and before-kth differ only in how you reach the target node; the splice is identical.
Before a given node is O(1) — the node itself supplies its predecessor via prev.
Skipping the successor's prev update is the classic silent corruption.

a2z-0239.intro: Bit manipulation treats an integer as a row of bits you can inspect and flip directly with AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts. It powers some of the most elegant constant-space tricks in all of DSA — finding the one non-repeated element, testing powers of two, counting set bits. This lesson covers the representation, the operators, the i-th bit toolkit, and the handful of classic tricks this module's problems are built from.

sections.h: Numbers as bits, and two's complement
sections.body:
An integer is stored in binary: 13 is 1101, meaning 8 + 4 + 0 + 1. Bit positions are counted from the right starting at 0, so bit i has value 2^i. A 32-bit int has bits 0..31.

Negative numbers use two's complement: invert all bits and add 1. In 8 bits, -1 is 11111111 and -2 is 11111110. Two consequences worth remembering: the sign lives in the most significant bit, and in fixed-width languages arithmetic wraps around. Python integers have arbitrary precision (conceptually infinitely many sign bits), which removes overflow surprises but means ~x is -x-1 and right-shifting a negative number keeps it negative.

AND (&) keeps bits set in both operands; OR (|) keeps bits set in either; XOR (^) keeps bits set in exactly one; NOT (~) flips every bit; left shift (<<) moves bits toward higher positions, multiplying by 2 per step; right shift (>>) moves them down, dividing by 2 (floor) per step for non-negative numbers.

XOR deserves special attention because three properties power half the tricks in this module: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and XOR is commutative and associative — order does not matter. That is why XOR-ing a whole array cancels every paired element and leaves the unpaired one.
sections.code:
a, b = 13, 10          # 1101 and 1010
print(a & b)           # 1000 = 8
print(a | b)           # 1111 = 15
print(a ^ b)           # 0111 = 7
print(a << 1)          # 11010 = 26  (multiply by 2)
print(a >> 1)          # 110  = 6    (divide by 2)

sections.body:
Everything is done with a mask — a number with a single 1 at position i, written (1 << i).

Check if bit i is set: (n >> i) & 1, or equivalently n & (1 << i) != 0. Set bit i: n | (1 << i). Clear bit i: n & ~(1 << i). Toggle bit i: n ^ (1 << i). Clear the lowest set bit: n & (n - 1) — subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 to 0 and all bits below it to 1, so the AND wipes exactly that bit. Isolate the lowest set bit: n & (-n).

sections.h: Classic tricks built from the toolkit
sections.body:
Odd or even: n & 1 — the last bit decides. Power of two: a power of two has exactly one set bit, so n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0. Count set bits (Brian Kernighan's algorithm): repeatedly clear the lowest set bit and count the steps — O(number of set bits) instead of O(32). Swap without a temp variable: a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b. Single non-repeated element: XOR the entire array; pairs annihilate.

Worked micro-example: counting set bits in 13 (1101): 13 & 12 = 12 (1100), count 1; 12 & 11 = 8 (1000), count 2; 8 & 7 = 0, count 3. Three set bits, three iterations.

(1) Operator precedence: in many languages == binds tighter than &, so (n & 1) == 1 needs its parentheses — Python included for comparisons against masks. (2) Using 1 << i with i = 31 in 32-bit signed languages overflows into the sign bit; use 1LL in C++ or long masks in Java. (3) Expecting >> on negative numbers to behave like division toward zero — it is an arithmetic shift (floor), and in C++ on negatives it was implementation-defined before C++20. (4) Trying bit tricks on problems that need counts — XOR cancels pairs but cannot tell you how many times something occurred; if elements appear three times (Single Number II), you need per-bit counting modulo 3 instead.

key_points: Bit i has value 2^i; a mask (1 << i) is how you address a single bit.
Check: (n >> i) & 1. Set: n | mask. Clear: n & ~mask. Toggle: n ^ mask.
n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit — powers of two and set-bit counting both come from this.
XOR properties x^x = 0 and x^0 = x make paired elements cancel — the single-number trick.
Watch precedence parentheses, shift widths in fixed-size languages, and negative-number shifts.

a2z-0267.intro: Sliding window and two pointers are the standard way to turn O(n^2) 'check every subarray' brute force into a single O(n) pass. The idea: maintain a window [left, right] over the array or string, expand right to include new elements, and shrink left whenever the window breaks the problem's condition. Because each index enters and leaves the window at most once, the whole scan is linear. This lesson covers the fixed and variable window patterns, the state you keep inside the window, and when the technique legally applies.

sections.body:
You hold two indices, left and right, delimiting a contiguous segment — the window. A driver loop advances right one step at a time, adding arr[right] to some running state (a sum, a frequency map, a count of distinct elements). Whenever the state violates the problem's condition, you advance left, removing arr[left] from the state, until the window is valid again. Every candidate answer is read off from valid windows.

The linearity argument is the thing to internalise: right moves at most n times total, and left also moves at most n times total (it never moves backward). So the loop body executes O(n) times overall, even though it contains a while loop inside a for loop.

When the window size K is given, the algorithm is mechanical: build the state for the first K elements, record the answer, then slide — remove the element leaving at the left, add the element entering at the right, record again — until right reaches the end.

Maximum sum of K consecutive elements and 'maximum points from cards' (where the window is the chunk you remove from the middle) are this pattern. Cost is O(n) time and O(1) to O(K) extra space depending on the state kept.
sections.code:
def max_sum_k(arr, k):
    window_sum = sum(arr[:k])
    best = window_sum
    for right in range(k, len(arr)):
        window_sum += arr[right]        # enter
        window_sum -= arr[right - k]    # leave
        best = max(best, window_sum)
    return best

sections.h: Pattern 2: variable window with a validity condition
sections.body:
When the size is not fixed, you expand right greedily and shrink left only while the window is invalid. The state usually includes a frequency map or a set so validity can be checked in O(1).

Worked example — longest substring without repeating characters in 'abcabcbb': expand over a, b, c (window 'abc', length 3). The next a repeats, so shrink from the left, removing a, until the window 'bca' is valid again. Continue: the window slides through 'cab', 'abc', then b repeats twice forcing shrinks to 'cb', then the final b forces 'b'. The maximum length seen is 3. Note the window content and its last-seen positions must be updated on both entry and exit — forgetting the exit update is the most common bug in this pattern.
sections.code:
def longest_without_repeat(s):
    seen = {}                 # char -> count in window
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        seen[ch] = seen.get(ch, 0) + 1
        while seen[ch] > 1:               # window invalid
            seen[s[left]] -= 1            # remove on exit
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

sections.body:
Many problems ask for subarrays with exactly K distinct elements, or sum exactly K, where a direct window cannot stop at 'exactly'. The standard reduction: count subarrays satisfying 'at most K', then answer exactly(K) = atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1). Inside atMost, whenever the window is valid, every subarray ending at right and starting anywhere in [left, right] is valid too, so you add (right - left + 1) to the count instead of just checking one length.

Two pointers on a sorted array is the sibling technique: pointers start at opposite ends and move toward each other based on a comparison (pair with given sum), or one pointer writes while another reads (remove duplicates, move zeroes). Same left/right discipline, different geometry.

sections.h: When it applies — and common mistakes
sections.body:
Sliding window requires monotonicity: extending the window must move the measured quantity in a predictable direction, and shrinking must be able to restore validity. It works for sums of non-negative numbers, distinctness, and character-frequency conditions. It fails when negatives make sums non-monotonic (use prefix sums + hashing instead) or when the condition involves ordering across the whole array.

Common mistakes: (1) not removing the leaving element from the state when shrinking; (2) using an if instead of a while for shrinking — one removal may not restore validity; (3) recording the answer before the window becomes valid; (4) in fixed-window code, an off-by-one in right - k when choosing the leaving element. Complexities: O(n) time; space O(1) for sums, O(distinct) for frequency states.

key_points: Each index enters and leaves the window at most once, so expand/shrink scans are O(n) despite the nested while.
Fixed window: build state for K elements, then add entering / remove leaving on each slide.
Variable window: expand right, shrink left with a while loop until the validity condition holds again.
exactly(K) = atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1) is the standard reduction for counting problems.
Requires monotonic behaviour — negative numbers break sum windows; switch to prefix sums + hashing there.

a2z-0280.intro: Stacks and queues are defined by their interfaces — LIFO and FIFO — not by how they are stored. This lesson is about building one structure out of another: a stack from two queues, a queue from two stacks, and both from arrays and linked lists. The point is fluency with the interfaces and honest cost analysis, including the amortised argument that makes the two-stack queue O(1) per operation even though one operation occasionally does O(n) work.

sections.body:
A stack offers push, pop, peek/top and isEmpty, all conceptually O(1), with last-in-first-out order. A queue offers enqueue (add at back), dequeue (remove from front), front/peek and isEmpty, all O(1), with first-in-first-out order.

An implementation is correct if the observable behaviour matches the interface, whatever happens inside. That freedom is what makes 'implement a queue using stacks' a meaningful exercise: internally you may move elements around, as long as dequeue returns elements in arrival order.

Keep an inbox stack and an outbox stack. Enqueue pushes onto inbox. Dequeue pops from outbox; if outbox is empty, first pour all of inbox into outbox (which reverses the order, putting the oldest element on top), then pop.

Why is this fast overall? Each element is pushed twice and popped twice in its entire lifetime — once in inbox, once in outbox. The expensive pour moves each element exactly once, so over n operations the total work is O(n): amortised O(1) per operation, even though a single dequeue after many enqueues costs O(n) once.

sections.h: Stack from queues, and the cost trade-off
sections.body:
With two queues (or even one), you choose which operation pays. Push-costly version: enqueue the new element, then rotate all older elements behind it, so the front of the queue is always the stack top — push is O(n), pop is O(1). Pop-costly version: enqueue is O(1) (just append at the back), and pop rotates all but the last element into the helper queue, removes the last, then swaps the queues' roles — pop is O(n).

There is no way to make both O(1) with plain queues; the exercise teaches you to read which operation the problem makes frequent and pay the cost on the other one.

Stack from an array: a top index; push writes at ++top, pop reads at top--. Watch overflow (fixed capacity) and underflow (popping empty). Queue from an array: a linear array wastes the slots freed at the front, so real implementations are circular — front and rear advance modulo capacity, with one slot (or a size counter) used to distinguish full from empty. Both directions of index arithmetic are classic off-by-one sources.

Linked-list versions remove capacity limits: a stack pushes/pops at the head (O(1), never use the tail); a queue enqueues at a maintained tail pointer and dequeues at the head, both O(1). Forgetting to update the tail pointer when the last element is dequeued is the standard bug — the next enqueue then attaches to a dead node.

Array stack/queue: O(1) per op, fixed capacity, circular indexing for queues. Linked-list versions: O(1) per op, O(n) total extra space in pointers, no capacity limit. Two-stack queue: amortised O(1), worst-case single op O(n). Two-queue stack: one operation is O(n) by design.

Common mistakes: pouring the inbox into the outbox while outbox still has elements (destroys order — only pour when outbox is empty); rotating the wrong count in the stack-from-queue push; and answering 'queue from two stacks is O(1)' without the word amortised in an interview.

key_points: Implementations must preserve the interface (LIFO / FIFO), not any particular internal layout.
Queue from two stacks: pour inbox into outbox only when outbox is empty; each element moves once, giving amortised O(1).
Stack from queues: either push or pop must pay O(n) — choose based on which operation dominates.
Array queues should be circular; linked-list queues need both head and tail pointers kept in sync.
Always state amortised vs worst-case honestly — a single two-stack dequeue can cost O(n).
