a2z-0311.intro: A binary tree is a hierarchy where each node holds a value and points to at most two children, left and right. Trees model everything from file systems to expression syntax to the recursion structure of divide-and-conquer, and they are the substrate for this whole module: traversals, views, diameters and constructions all assume you are fluent in the vocabulary and the node representation. This lesson builds that foundation before the traversal drills begin.

sections.h: Vocabulary: the parts of a tree
sections.body:
The root is the single node with no parent. A node's children are its left and right successors; nodes with no children are leaves. The depth of a node is the number of edges from the root to it (root depth 0); the height of a node is the longest downward path to a leaf, and the height of the tree is the height of its root — beware that some sources count nodes instead of edges, shifting every figure by one, so fix the convention before comparing answers.

A subtree is a node together with all its descendants. Ancestors of a node are the nodes on the path from the root down to its parent. Almost every recursive tree algorithm is phrased as: solve for the left subtree, solve for the right subtree, combine at the current node.

Full: every node has 0 or 2 children. Perfect: full, and all leaves at the same depth — a perfect tree of height h has 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes. Complete: every level except possibly the last is full, and the last level fills left to right — this is the shape heaps use, and it guarantees height O(log n). Balanced: left and right subtree heights differ by at most 1 everywhere (AVL-style), also O(log n) height. Degenerate (skewed): every node has one child — the tree is a linked list in disguise with height O(n).

Height is the master variable: most tree algorithms are O(n) time, but their recursion depth — and BST operation costs — are governed by height, which swings between log n (complete/balanced) and n (skewed) for the same node count.

sections.h: Representation: nodes, and building from level order
sections.body: The standard representation mirrors the linked list: a node object with data, left and right references (None for missing children). Problems often give input as a level-order array (breadth-first listing, with nulls for gaps); converting it to nodes uses a queue — pop a node, attach the next two array values as its children, enqueue non-null children.

Visiting every node exactly once is a traversal. Depth-first traversals are defined by when the root is processed relative to its subtrees: preorder (root, left, right), inorder (left, root, right), postorder (left, right, root). Breadth-first traversal processes level by level using a queue — the same order as the array representation above.

On the tree with root 1, left subtree 2 (children 4, 5) and right child 3: preorder is 1 2 4 5 3; inorder is 4 2 5 1 3; postorder is 4 5 2 3 1; level order is 1 2 3 4 5. The next lessons drill each of these recursively and iteratively; here, just be able to produce all four by hand for a small tree.

Any traversal visits each node once: O(n) time. Extra space is O(h) for the recursion stack in DFS (h = height, so O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed) and O(width) for the BFS queue, which is O(n) for a perfect tree's last level.

Common mistakes: (1) mixing up height conventions (edges vs nodes) and being off by one on depth/height questions; (2) calling a tree complete when it is only full, or vice versa; (3) assuming a binary tree is sorted — the ordering property belongs to the binary SEARCH tree, covered in the next module; (4) forgetting that in level-order input, children of null nodes are not present in the array — the builder above only consumes values for nodes actually dequeued, which is the convention most judges use.

key_points: Node = data + left + right; fix your height convention (edges vs nodes) before answering.
Perfect and complete trees have height O(log n); a degenerate tree is a list with height O(n) — height drives costs.
Complete means last level fills left to right; full means 0 or 2 children everywhere — they are different properties.
Traversals: preorder (root-L-R), inorder (L-root-R), postorder (L-R-root), level order (BFS with a queue).
Level-order arrays are converted to nodes with a queue; nulls have no children entries in the input.

a2z-0343.intro: A binary search tree (BST) adds one ordering rule to a binary tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger. That single invariant turns blind O(n) searching into a guided walk that discards half the tree at each step — O(log n) on balanced shapes. This lesson covers the invariant, the three core operations (search, insert, delete), and why the inorder traversal of a BST is always sorted.

sections.body:
For every node N: every value in N's left subtree is less than N's value, and every value in N's right subtree is greater. The condition is about entire subtrees, not just immediate children — a node can satisfy both children locally yet violate an ancestor's bound, which is exactly why validating a BST needs a (min, max) range passed down, not just parent-child checks.

Duplicates need a policy: most problem statements here assume distinct values; when duplicates exist, decide whether they go left or right and apply it consistently, since search and delete depend on it.

Start at the root. If the target equals the node value, done. If it is smaller, the invariant guarantees it can only live in the left subtree; if larger, only in the right. Move down and repeat; falling off the tree (reaching None) means absent.

Each step discards one whole subtree, so the cost is O(h) where h is the height: O(log n) for balanced trees, O(n) for a skewed one — inserting sorted data into a plain BST builds exactly that worst case, which is why self-balancing variants (AVL, red-black) exist in libraries.

Insert is search with a purpose: walk down as if searching; when you fall off the tree, attach the new node at that empty spot. It automatically lands in the only position that preserves the invariant. New nodes are always leaves.

Delete has three cases. Leaf: just remove it. One child: replace the node with that child. Two children: copy the inorder successor's value (the smallest value in the right subtree — step right once, then left to the bottom) into the node, then delete that successor node instead; the successor has at most a right child, so its deletion is one of the easy cases. All three operations are O(h).

Do an inorder traversal (left, root, right) of a BST and the values come out in ascending order — a direct consequence of the invariant, provable by induction on the tree. This one fact powers a family of problems in this module: k-th smallest is the k-th element of the inorder walk; validating a BST can be done by checking the inorder sequence is strictly increasing; two-sum in a BST uses two inorder iterators (one ascending, one descending) as two pointers.

It also explains floor and ceil: while searching, keep the best candidate seen so far — the last node where you turned right is the floor candidate, symmetrically for ceil.

Search, insert and delete are all O(h) time and O(1) iterative space (O(h) if recursive). Balanced: O(log n). Skewed: O(n) — a plain BST gives no balance guarantee.

Common mistakes: (1) validating with only local child comparisons instead of propagated min/max bounds; (2) in the two-children delete, copying the successor value but forgetting to then delete the successor node, duplicating it; (3) choosing the inorder predecessor vs successor inconsistently (either works if applied fully); (4) assuming insert keeps the tree balanced — it never rebalances, so input order determines shape; sorted input is the pathological case.

key_points: Invariant: left subtree values < node < right subtree values, for every node, over whole subtrees.
Search/insert/delete all cost O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed — a plain BST does not self-balance.
Delete's hard case (two children) reduces to copying the inorder successor, then deleting that node.
Inorder traversal of a BST yields sorted order — the master key for k-th smallest, validation and two-sum problems.
Validate with propagated (min, max) bounds, not just parent-child comparisons.

a2z-0358.intro: A heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that maintains one promise: every parent is smaller than its children (min-heap) or larger (max-heap). That partial order is exactly what a priority queue needs — the extreme element is always at the root, reachable in O(1), with insert and extract in O(log n). This lesson covers the array representation, the two repair operations (bubble up and heapify down), and how building a heap from an array is O(n), not O(n log n).

sections.body:
A heap obeys two rules. Shape: it is a complete binary tree — every level full except possibly the last, which fills left to right — so its height is always floor(log n). Order: for a min-heap, each node's value is less than or equal to its children's; a max-heap reverses the comparison.

Notice what a heap does NOT promise: siblings are unordered relative to each other, and the tree is not sorted — an inorder traversal of a heap is not a sorted sequence. It is a weaker (and therefore cheaper to maintain) structure than a BST, optimised for exactly one query: give me the min (or max), repeatedly.

Because the tree is complete, it packs into an array with no gaps and no pointers. With 0-based indexing, node i has parent (i - 1) // 2 and children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. The root sits at index 0, the last element at index n - 1, and the last internal node (parent) is at index n//2 - 1.

Getting these formulas wrong — usually by mixing in the 1-based versions (parent i//2, children 2i, 2i+1) — is the most frequent heap bug. Pick one convention per codebase and stick to it.
sections.code:
def parent(i): return (i - 1) // 2
def left(i):   return 2 * i + 1
def right(i):  return 2 * i + 2

# min-heap as a Python list: heap[0] is always the minimum

sections.h: The two repair moves: bubble up and heapify down
sections.body:
Insert appends the new element at the end (preserving shape) and bubbles it up: while it is smaller than its parent, swap. Extract-min saves the root, moves the last element to the root (preserving shape), and heapifies down: repeatedly swap it with its smaller child until both children are larger or it reaches a leaf. Both moves travel one root-to-leaf path, so both are O(log n); peek is O(1).

Decrease-key / arbitrary updates use the same moves: if the value decreased, bubble up; if it increased, heapify down. Choosing the wrong direction is a classic bug — after an update you must consider which way the element can possibly be out of order.

sections.h: Building a heap in O(n), and heap sort
sections.body:
Inserting n elements one by one costs O(n log n). The faster build: copy the array as-is (shape property already satisfied by any array), then call heapify_down on every internal node from the last parent (index n//2 - 1) down to the root. Most nodes sit near the leaves and move down only a step or two, and the total work sums to O(n) — a result worth being able to sketch: sum over heights of (number of nodes) x (max sink distance) converges to about 2n swaps.

Heap sort reuses this: build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root (current maximum) to the end of the shrinking array and heapify down the reduced heap. Result: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space, but not stable.

Peek O(1); push and pop O(log n); build O(n); space O(n) in the array itself. Reach for a heap when the problem says top-K, k-th largest, merge many sorted streams, continuously extract min/max, or maintain a running median (two heaps). If you need arbitrary search or deletion of a named element, a heap is the wrong tool (those are O(n) without an index map).

Common mistakes: mixing 0-based and 1-based index formulas; heapifying only downward after an operation that requires bubbling up; assuming heap order implies sorted order when iterating; and in Python, forgetting that heapq is a min-heap only — negate values for max-heap behaviour, and use heapq.heapify for the O(n) build instead of pushing in a loop.

key_points: Heap = complete binary tree in an array + parent-before-children order; only the root (the extreme) is guaranteed.
0-based indices: parent (i-1)//2, children 2i+1 and 2i+2 — never mix with the 1-based formulas.
Insert = append + bubble up; extract = move last to root + heapify down. Both O(log n); peek O(1).
Build by heapifying from the last parent down to the root: O(n) total, beating n inserts.
Heaps answer 'extreme value, repeatedly' — top-K, k-way merge, streaming median — not search or sorted iteration.

a2z-0378.intro: A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges — the most general structure in this course, since trees, linked lists and grids are all special cases. Graphs model networks, maps, dependencies and states, and nearly every problem in this module is a traversal or a shortest-path variant on one of two representations. This lesson fixes the vocabulary and the representations so the algorithm lessons that follow have solid ground.

sections.body:
A graph G = (V, E): V vertices (nodes), E edges connecting pairs of them. An edge is undirected (a two-way road) or directed (a one-way street, drawn with an arrow). Edges may carry weights (distances, costs). The degree of a vertex is the number of edges touching it (in-degree and out-degree when directed).

A path is a sequence of vertices joined by edges; a cycle is a path that returns to its start. A graph with no cycles is acyclic — a tree is exactly a connected acyclic undirected graph, equivalently n nodes and n-1 edges. Two vertices are connected if a path joins them; a connected component is a maximal set of mutually connected vertices. A graph where every pair is directly joined is complete. Internalising these words matters because problem statements are written in them: 'provinces', 'islands', 'prerequisites' are components and DAGs in costume.

Three input shapes cover almost everything. (1) n and an edge list — pairs (u, v), sometimes with weights (u, v, w). (2) An adjacency structure given directly. (3) An implicit graph: a grid where each cell is a vertex connected to its up/down/left/right neighbours (islands, flood fill, rotten oranges), or a state graph where vertices are configurations (word ladder).

Also settle indexing early: vertices may be labelled 0..n-1 or 1..n. Mismatching this against your arrays is the single most common cause of graph bugs, so convert once at input time.

An n x n table where matrix[u][v] = 1 (or the weight) if edge u-v exists, else 0 / infinity. Checking whether an edge exists is O(1), but the table costs O(n^2) space regardless of how few edges exist, and listing a vertex's neighbours costs O(n) — you must scan its entire row.

Matrices suit dense graphs and small n, and they arise naturally when the input itself is a grid or a matrix (in grid problems you usually do not build the matrix as a graph at all — the grid is the graph, with neighbours computed on the fly).
sections.code:
# adjacency matrix for an undirected unweighted graph
n = 5
mat = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
for u, v in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]:
    mat[u][v] = 1
    mat[v][u] = 1     # undirected: record both directions

sections.body:
For each vertex, store the list of its neighbours (with weights as tuples when needed). Space is O(V + E), listing neighbours of u costs O(degree(u)), and traversals over the whole graph cost O(V + E) — the standard complexity you will quote for BFS and DFS. This is the default representation for this module.

For undirected graphs, add each edge to both endpoints' lists; forgetting the reverse entry silently turns your graph directed and breaks connectivity answers.
sections.code:
def build_adj_list(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:               # unweighted, undirected
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    return adj

def build_weighted_adj_list(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:            # directed, weighted
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    return adj

sections.h: Traversal mental model and common mistakes
sections.body:
Two traversals organise everything. BFS explores level by level with a queue — on unweighted graphs it also yields shortest paths in edges. DFS dives down one path with a stack or recursion — natural for components, cycles and topological order. Both mark vertices in a visited array the moment they are enqueued/pushed (not when popped), or the same vertex gets queued many times.

Common mistakes: (1) forgetting the visited array entirely and looping forever on the first cycle; (2) marking visited at pop time, flooding the queue with duplicates; (3) adding undirected edges in one direction only; (4) 0-index vs 1-index mismatches between the edge list and your arrays; (5) running a traversal from vertex 0 only and missing other components — wrap it in a loop over all vertices.

key_points: Graph = vertices + edges; directed vs undirected and weighted vs unweighted are the first two questions to ask of any problem.
A tree is a connected acyclic graph: n vertices, n-1 edges — graph algorithms generalise tree ones.
Adjacency list is the default: O(V + E) space and traversal. Adjacency matrix: O(1) edge check but O(V^2) space.
Undirected edges go into both endpoints' lists; directed edges go in one.
Visited must be marked when a vertex is enqueued, and traversals must be restarted for every unvisited component.

a2z-0413.intro: A minimum spanning tree (MST) is the cheapest set of edges that connects every vertex of a weighted undirected graph — the answer to 'link all these points with minimum total cable/road cost'. This lesson covers what a spanning tree is, the cut property that justifies both classic algorithms, and how Prim's and Kruskal's each build the MST, including the disjoint-set structure Kruskal's depends on.

sections.h: Spanning trees and minimum spanning trees
sections.body:
A spanning tree of a connected graph with V vertices is a subgraph that includes all V vertices, is connected, and has no cycles — which forces exactly V - 1 edges. Drop any one of those properties and it is not a spanning tree.

Many spanning trees usually exist; the MST is the one whose total edge weight is smallest. If the graph is disconnected, no spanning tree exists — instead each component gets its own MST, forming a minimum spanning forest. Edge weights need not be distances; any cost works, and negative weights are fine (unlike shortest-path algorithms, MST algorithms do not care).

sections.h: The cut property — the one idea behind both algorithms
sections.body:
A cut splits the vertices into two groups. An edge crossing the cut connects the groups. The cut property states: the minimum-weight edge crossing any cut is safe — it belongs to some MST (to every MST, if its weight is unique).

Both algorithms are this theorem applied repeatedly. Prim's grows one group (the tree built so far) and takes the cheapest edge leaving it. Kruskal's considers edges in increasing order; adding the cheapest edge that connects two different components is safe because that edge is the minimum crossing the cut between its component and the rest. When you are stuck proving or debugging an MST solution, come back to this property.

Steps: sort all edges by weight ascending; walk through them, adding an edge whenever its endpoints are in different components, and merging those components; stop after V - 1 edges are added.

The 'different components?' test must be near-constant time, which is the disjoint set union (DSU) structure's job: find(x) returns the component's representative, with path compression flattening the tree as it goes; union(a, b) merges by size or rank. With both optimisations, operations are amortised almost O(1). Sorting dominates the cost: O(E log E) overall.

Prim's grows a single tree from a start vertex. Maintain a min-heap of candidate edges (weight, to-vertex) leaving the visited set, plus a visited array. Repeatedly pop the cheapest candidate; if its far endpoint is unvisited, that edge joins the MST, the vertex becomes visited, and all its outgoing edges are pushed. Continue until V - 1 edges are chosen.

Cost with a binary heap is O(E log V). Prim's is usually preferred for dense graphs (many edges, where Kruskal's sort of a huge edge list dominates) and when the graph is given as an adjacency list; Kruskal's is simpler when you already have an edge list. Worked check: vertices 1-4 with edges 1-2 (1), 2-3 (2), 1-3 (4), 3-4 (1), 2-4 (5). Kruskal takes 1-2 (1), then 3-4 (1), then 2-3 (2) — total 4 — and correctly skips 1-3 (4) because 1 and 3 are already connected through 1-2-3.

sections.h: MST vs shortest path, and common mistakes
sections.body:
Do not confuse the MST with shortest paths from a source: Dijkstra minimises the distance from one root to each vertex; an MST minimises the total weight of the whole tree, and the path between two vertices inside an MST is generally not their shortest path. The algorithms look similar (both use heaps and greedily take cheap edges) but optimise different quantities — an interview favourite.

Common mistakes: (1) running Kruskal without sorting, or stopping before checking that V - 1 edges were actually added (disconnected input); (2) a DSU find without path compression degrading on long chains; (3) in Prim's, pushing edges but forgetting the visited check on pop, which adds cycle-forming edges; (4) assuming the MST is unique — it is unique only if all edge weights are distinct; equal weights can give several MSTs with the same total weight.

key_points: A spanning tree connects all V vertices with exactly V - 1 edges and no cycles; the MST minimises total weight.
Cut property: the cheapest edge crossing any cut is always safe to include — both algorithms are this rule applied repeatedly.
Kruskal: sort edges, add those joining different DSU components; O(E log E), dominated by the sort.
Prim: grow one tree with a min-heap of frontier edges; O(E log V), better for dense graphs.
MST total weight is unique even when the tree is not; MST paths are not shortest paths — that is Dijkstra's job.

a2z-0424.intro: Dynamic programming (DP) is recursion with a memory: when a problem breaks into subproblems that repeat, solve each distinct subproblem once, store its answer, and reuse it. That single change routinely converts exponential brute force into polynomial time — Fibonacci goes from O(2^n) to O(n). This lesson gives you the recognition test for DP, the five-step recipe, and the three implementation styles (memoization, tabulation, space-optimised) on one running example.

sections.h: When DP applies: the two properties
sections.body:
A problem is DP-shaped when it has (1) overlapping subproblems — the recursion tree revisits the same smaller problems many times — and (2) optimal substructure — an optimal answer is assembled from optimal answers of those subproblems (true for counting and min/max problems where choices decompose cleanly).

Contrast with divide and conquer (merge sort): its subproblems are disjoint, so there is nothing to reuse and DP adds nothing. Contrast with greedy: greedy commits to one locally best choice and never revisits it; DP systematically considers choices but caches their results. If you can draw the recursion tree and see repeated nodes, DP will help.

sections.h: The Fibonacci story: from exponential to linear
sections.body:
Naive fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) recomputes fib(n-2) twice, fib(n-3) three times, and so on — the call tree has O(2^n) nodes even though there are only n+1 distinct subproblems (fib(0) .. fib(n)).

Memoization (top-down): keep a cache; before computing, check it; after computing, store. Each distinct subproblem is now solved once: O(n) time, O(n) space for cache plus recursion stack. Tabulation (bottom-up): fill a table from the base cases upward in dependency order — fib[0], fib[1], then each fib[i] = fib[i-1] + fib[i-2]. Same O(n) time, no recursion. Space optimisation: since fib[i] depends only on the previous two values, keep two variables instead of the table — O(1) space. Recognising what a state actually depends on is how most DP solutions shed their table at the end.

Every DP in this module can be produced mechanically:

1. Define the state: what does dp[...] mean, in one sentence? ('dp[i] = maximum sum obtainable considering the first i elements.') The state variables are the things that change across subproblems — an index, a capacity, a previous choice.
2. Write the recurrence: express dp[state] using smaller states, mirroring the choices at each step (take / skip, come from up / left, etc.
3. Fix the base cases: the smallest states answered directly.
4. Choose the computation order so every dependency is ready (for tabulation) — usually increasing index; for 2D, by rows.
5. Locate the answer: which state is the final result? (Not always dp[n] — sometimes a max over a row.)

If you cannot state step 1 in one sentence, the state is wrong or missing a dimension — that is the signal to add the missing variable (for example, 'previous element taken or not' in house-robber style problems).

Problem: count ways to reach step n taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. State: ways(i) = number of ways to reach step i. Recurrence: the last move was a single step from i-1 or a double from i-2, so ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2). Base: ways(0) = 1 (already there), ways(1) = 1. Answer: ways(n). This is Fibonacci wearing a costume — and that recognition skill (this new problem is that solved problem) is most of what 'being good at DP' means in practice.

Complexity formula for any DP: (number of distinct states) x (cost per state transition). Here n states x O(1) transition = O(n). Quote complexities this way in interviews and use it to sanity-check whether your state design is feasible.

(1) A state definition that secretly depends on history not captured in the state — answers then differ for the 'same' state and caching is wrong. (2) Base cases off by one, especially dp[0]: decide whether it means 'empty input' and be consistent. (3) In tabulation, iterating in an order where dependencies are not yet computed (for example, knapsack's 0/1 items require iterating capacity backwards — iterating forwards silently reuses the same item twice and solves the unbounded variant). (4) Forgetting the required modulo (usually 10^9 + 7) on counting problems. (5) Deep recursion in top-down solutions hitting recursion limits on large n — switch to tabulation or raise the limit deliberately.

key_points: DP = recursion + caching, applicable when subproblems overlap and optimal answers compose from optimal sub-answers.
Memoization is top-down with a cache; tabulation is bottom-up in dependency order; both are O(states x transition).
The five steps: define state in one sentence, recurrence, base cases, order, locate the answer.
If the same subproblem can be reached with different histories that matter, your state is missing a variable.
Space optimisation: keep only the previous row / last few values the recurrence actually reads.

a2z-0477.intro: Before tackling maximum-XOR problems with a trie, you need the bit-level groundwork this lesson assembles: how numbers decompose into bits, why XOR behaves like addition without carry, and how a binary trie — a trie whose alphabet is just {0, 1} — stores numbers bit by bit from the most significant bit down. With those pieces, the greedy 'prefer the opposite bit' walk that maximises XOR stops being a trick and becomes obvious.

sections.h: The XOR facts you will actually use
sections.body:
XOR compares numbers bit by bit, independently per position — there is no carry. Three identities drive everything: x ^ x = 0 (a number cancels itself), x ^ 0 = x, and XOR is commutative and associative, so a ^ b ^ a = b. A fourth observation matters for maximisation: a 1 in a high bit outweighs 1s in all lower bits combined (2^k > 2^k - 1 = sum of all lower bits), so when building an answer bit by bit, greedy choices at high positions are always safe.

Also useful: the XOR of a range or set can be maintained incrementally — inserting or removing a value is just XOR-ing it in, since x ^ x = 0 removes it again.

sections.h: From character tries to binary tries
sections.body:
A regular trie stores strings: each node has children indexed by character, and a root-to-leaf path spells a prefix. Replace the alphabet with bits: each node has exactly two children, child[0] and child[1]. Inserting a number means walking from the most significant bit to the least, creating nodes as needed. Every number of the same bit-width follows a path of identical length (say 32), so all leaves sit at the same depth.

Fix the bit width in advance — commonly bit 31 down to bit 0 for non-negative values up to about 2^31, so numbers align by magnitude: their highest bits are all compared at the same trie levels, which is what makes the greedy walk below valid. Nodes commonly store a count of how many inserted numbers pass through them; that count is what later problems use for 'how many numbers give XOR less than K' style queries.

Given x, find the inserted number y maximising x ^ y. Walk the trie alongside x's bits from high to low. At bit b, your result gets a 1 at position b exactly when y has the opposite bit to x there. So greedily prefer the child labelled 1 - (x's bit); take it if it exists. If it does not, you are forced into the same-bit child and that answer bit is 0. Because high bits dominate (the fact from section 1), never sacrificing a high 1 for any combination of lower bits is provably optimal.

Worked example: inserted numbers include 9 (01001) and 5 (00101), query x = 12 (01100), using 5 bits. Bit 4: x has 0, prefer child 1 — none exist (all numbers start 0), take 0. Bit 3: x has 1, prefer 0 — 5's path qualifies, follow it. Remaining bits follow 5's path: answer bits so far 1 at bit 3; bits 2..0 of the walk against 5 (00101) vs x (01100) give XOR bits 0,0,1... computing fully: 12 ^ 5 = 9, while 12 ^ 9 = 5, so the walk correctly selects y = 5 with XOR 9. Insert and query each cost O(bits) = O(32) — effectively constant.

(1) Inserting bits from least significant upward — the trie then groups numbers by their low bits, magnitude alignment is destroyed, and the greedy walk is invalid. Always MSB first. (2) Inconsistent bit width between insert and query: if one number was inserted over 31 bits and queried over 20, the paths do not line up. (3) Forgetting the count field until a problem asks for counting queries (XOR less than K, pairs with XOR in a range) and having to rebuild the structure. (4) Signed values: for possibly negative numbers in fixed-width languages, two's complement makes the sign bit behave like any other bit if you consistently use the full width (e., 32 bits) — problems in this module use non-negative values, so 31..0 is safe.

key_points: XOR is per-bit with no carry: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, order irrelevant — and a high 1 beats all lower bits combined.
A binary trie stores numbers MSB-first; each node has children for bit 0 and bit 1 plus a pass-through count.
Max-XOR query: at each bit prefer the child opposite to x's bit; fall back to the same bit only when forced.
Insert and query are O(number of bits) — treat 32-bit widths as constant time.
Keep insert and query bit-widths identical, and include node counts from the start for counting queries.

a2z-0487.intro: String hashing converts any substring into a number (its hash) such that equal strings hash equally, letting you compare substrings in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing instead of O(length) character by character. It is the engine inside Rabin-Karp pattern matching and a fast — if probabilistic — alternative to exact algorithms like KMP and Z-function. This lesson derives the polynomial rolling hash, shows the O(1) substring-hash formula with a worked example, and explains collisions and how double hashing controls them.

sections.h: The polynomial hash and prefix hashes
sections.body:
Map each character to a small positive integer (a=1, b=2, ..., or use its code). Choose a base B (a random small odd number like 31 or 9113823; commonly 31 for lowercase letters) and a large prime modulus M (like 1,000,000,007). The prefix hash is defined by H[0] = 0 and H[i+1] = (H[i] * B + val(s[i])) mod M. So H[i] is the hash of the first i characters, interpreted as digits in base B.

Because the string is being read as a base-B number, appending a character is one multiply-add — and, crucially, a prefix can be 'subtracted' to isolate any substring, as the next section shows. Precompute powers B^0 .. B^n mod M once alongside H.
sections.code:
MOD = 1_000_000_007
BASE = 31

def build_hash(s):
    n = len(s)
    H = [0] * (n + 1)
    P = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        v = ord(ch) - ord('a') + 1      # 1..26, never 0
        H[i + 1] = (H[i] * BASE + v) % MOD
        P[i + 1] = (P[i] * BASE) % MOD
    return H, P

def substring_hash(H, P, l, r):
    # hash of s[l:r] in O(1)
    return (H[r] - H[l] * P[r - l]) % MOD

sections.h: Why the substring formula works — worked example
sections.body:
H[r] contains the whole prefix as a base-B number; the part before l sits in the high positions, multiplied by B^(r-l). Subtracting H[l] * B^(r-l) removes exactly that leading part, leaving the value of s[l:r] as if it started at position 0. Take s = 'abcd' with B = 10 and no modulus for readability (values a=1..d=4): H = [0, 1, 12, 123, 1234]. Hash of 'bc' (l=1, r=3): H[3] - H[1] * 10^2 = 123 - 100 = 23 — and indeed 'bc' read directly is 2*10 + 3 = 23. In code, always take % MOD after subtraction and add MOD if negative (Python's % already returns non-negative for positive modulus).

With this, comparing two substrings for equality, finding the longest repeated substring (binary search length + hash set), or checking palindromes (compare forward and reverse-string hashes) all become O(1)-per-comparison tasks.

Different strings can share a hash — a collision — either by bad luck or because a problem setter engineered test data against a known base/modulus pair (hash flooding). A single 1e9+7 modulus makes accidental collisions unlikely (roughly one in a billion per comparison), but adversarial cases exist, so the standard defences are: (1) double hashing — compute two hashes with different mod primes (1e9+7 and 1e9+9) or different bases and compare pairs, squaring the safety; (2) use a random base chosen at runtime; (3) in Python, skip the modulus and let arbitrary-precision integers hold the full base-B value, reducing collisions to zero for practical string lengths (at some speed cost) — effectively a 2^64 natural-overflow hash is another common choice in C++ (unsigned long long overflow) with a random odd base.

Character values must start at 1, not 0: with a=0, the strings 'a' and 'aa' would both hash to 0, and leading 'a's would be invisible to the hash.

To find a pattern P (length m) in a text T (length n): hash P once, then compare it against the hash of every length-m window of T using the O(1) substring formula. On a hash match, verify character by character (or trust double hashing). Expected total time is O(n + m) — versus O(n*m) naive scanning — because almost every window is rejected by its hash in O(1).

Know the neighbourhood: KMP and Z-function solve the same matching problem exactly in O(n + m) with no collision risk, which is why they have their own lessons in this module. Hashing wins when you need arbitrary substring equality, not just pattern search — repeated substrings, palindrome checks, longest common substring of two strings — where prefix-function methods do not directly apply.

(1) Using character value 0 for 'a', making leading characters invisible. (2) Forgetting to precompute powers up to n, or indexing P with the wrong length (r - l, not r - l + 1 in this half-open convention) — pick one interval convention and test it on a 1-character substring. (3) Negative intermediate results in languages whose % can return negatives; add MOD before the final %. (4) Trusting a single fixed base/modulus in judged problems known for anti-hash tests — randomise the base or double-hash. (5) Overflow in fixed-width languages when multiplying two mod-sized numbers: use 64-bit intermediates (1e9 * 1e9 fits in 64 bits, not 32).

key_points: Prefix polynomial hash: H[i+1] = (H[i]*B + val) mod M turns any substring into a base-B number.
Substring hash in O(1): H[r] - H[l] * B^(r-l) mod M — precompute powers once.
Character values start at 1; a 0 value makes leading characters disappear from the hash.
Collisions are the price: control them with double hashing, a random base, or 64-bit natural overflow.
Rabin-Karp uses window hashes for O(n + m) expected matching; hashing also serves substring equality, repeats and palindromes where KMP/Z do not apply.

a2z-0001.intro: Almost every beginner secretly believes programming belongs to a special breed of people — maths toppers, kids who coded at age ten, or 'geniuses'. That belief, not a lack of talent, is what makes most students quit DSA before they start. This lesson names the myths, shows what skill at programming actually comes from, and gives you a realistic way to begin.

sections.h: The five myths that stop beginners
sections.body:
Myth 1: 'Only geniuses can code.' Professional programmers are not doing genius-level thinking all day; they are applying a few dozen well-practised patterns. What looks like genius from outside is usually just pattern recognition built by repetition.

Myth 2: 'I must be great at mathematics.' School-level comfort with numbers — divisibility, remainders, powers, basic counting — covers almost everything in beginner and intermediate DSA. Advanced maths appears only in specialised topics, and you learn it when you reach them.

Myth 3: 'I have to memorise all the syntax.' Nobody memorises a language. You remember the 20% you use daily and look up the rest. Exams and interviews test problem solving, not recall of rare functions.

Myth 4: 'It is too late to start.' Placement preparation is measured in months of focused practice, not years of childhood hobby coding. Students routinely go from zero to interview-ready in 6–9 months of consistent work.

Myth 5: 'I need the perfect setup and course first.' A laptop, one language, and one structured sheet are enough. Endless preparation to start is procrastination in disguise.

Three things, all trainable. First, decomposition: breaking a scary problem into small steps you already know how to do. Second, pattern vocabulary: two pointers, sliding window, hashing, recursion and a few dozen other ideas recur in hundreds of problems — each one you learn unlocks a whole family. Third, debugging stamina: the patience to trace a wrong answer calmly instead of restarting randomly.

Notice what is absent from that list: IQ, school marks, and how early you started. Consistency beats intensity — one problem a day for a year teaches far more than forty problems in one exhausted weekend, because spaced repetition is what moves patterns into long-term memory.

Learn a concept briefly, then immediately solve 3–5 easy problems on it. If you get stuck for more than 30–40 minutes, read the idea (not the full code), close it, and write the solution yourself. Re-solve the same problem after a week without looking — if you can redo it, you own it; if not, it goes back into the loop.

Keep a small mistake notebook: the problem, what you missed (an edge case, a wrong formula, a complexity trap), and the one-line fix. Reviewing your own repeated mistakes is the fastest known shortcut in this field.

Treat every error message and wrong answer as information, not judgement. Compare yourself only with last month's version of you. Expect the first two weeks to feel slow — you are building the vocabulary that later makes everything faster. The students who succeed are simply the ones who did not stop.

key_points: Programming skill is trained pattern recognition, not inborn genius.
Beginner DSA needs only school-level maths: remainders, divisibility, powers, counting.
Nobody memorises syntax — you internalise the common 20% and look up the rest.
Consistency (daily practice) beats intensity (weekend marathons) because of spaced repetition.
Use the loop: learn briefly, solve easy problems, review the idea when stuck, re-solve after a week.
A mistake notebook turns every failure into a permanent upgrade.

a2z-0002.intro: Before writing programs it helps to know what a computer actually is and what it does with your code. A computer is not intelligent — it is an extremely fast, extremely obedient machine that executes simple instructions exactly as given. Understanding this model explains almost everything that follows in DSA: why algorithms are written as precise steps, and why we care about time and memory at all.

sections.body:
Strip away the screen and apps and a computer does four things: it takes input (keyboard, files, sensors), processes it, stores data, and produces output. The processing is done by the CPU, which performs billions of tiny operations per second — add these two numbers, compare those two numbers, copy this value — each one laughably simple, but executed at staggering speed.

Two kinds of memory matter to you. RAM (main memory) is fast, temporary working space where your program's variables live while it runs; it is wiped when the program ends. Storage (SSD/hard disk) is slow but permanent. A core idea in DSA is that RAM is limited, so how much of it your algorithm uses (space complexity) genuinely matters.

A program is a precise sequence of instructions that tells the computer how to transform input into output. Three related words are worth separating now:

An algorithm is the idea — the step-by-step recipe, independent of any language. A program is that recipe written in a programming language. The running process is the program actually executing, with real data in memory.

Computers have zero judgement: they do exactly what you said, not what you meant. Almost every bug you will ever meet is a gap between those two things, which is why the field rewards precision and careful tracing.

sections.h: How your code reaches the CPU
sections.body:
You write source code in a language like C++, Java or Python, but the CPU only understands machine code — binary instructions. A compiler (C++, Java) translates your whole program to machine code before it runs; an interpreter (Python) translates and executes it piece by piece while it runs, which is more flexible but slower.

While running, each variable is a named box in RAM holding a value. When you write x = x + 1, the CPU reads the value in box x, adds 1, and stores the result back. Keeping this 'boxes and instructions' picture in your head makes loops, arrays and recursion far easier to reason about later.

Every algorithm you write is ultimately a budget of CPU operations and RAM boxes. 'Optimising' means spending fewer of both. When an interviewer asks for a better solution, they are asking: can you get the same output with fewer operations, or less memory? Time and space complexity — which you meet properly in the Time Complexity lesson — are just disciplined ways of counting these two budgets before you run anything.

key_points: A computer = input, processing (CPU), memory (RAM + storage), output — fast and literal, never smart.
An algorithm is the language-independent recipe; a program is that recipe written in code.
Compilers translate everything up front (C++/Java); interpreters translate while running (Python).
Variables are named boxes in RAM; execution is the CPU reading, computing and storing, billions of times per second.
DSA optimisation = fewer CPU operations and fewer memory boxes for the same result.

a2z-0003.intro: Staring at a problem and feeling blank is not a talent problem — it is a process problem. Programmers who look 'naturally good' are running a quiet checklist in their heads: understand, break down, start with a dumb solution, look for the pattern, then refine. This lesson makes that checklist explicit so you can run it deliberately on every problem in this sheet.

sections.body:
First, restate the problem in your own words and pin down the exact input and output with one concrete example. Most 'I don't know where to start' moments are actually 'I haven't understood what is being asked' moments.

Then decompose: split the goal into sub-tasks you already know. 'Check if a number is a palindrome' becomes: reverse the number (a loop you know), then compare two values (trivial). Almost every hard problem is a chain of easy sub-problems wearing a costume; your job is to find the seams.

sections.h: Step 3: Solve it by hand first
sections.body: Before writing any code, do two or three examples on paper with actual numbers. Write the intermediate values down. The mechanical steps you find yourself repeating are your loop; the values you keep track of are your variables; the condition you check before stopping is your loop condition. Code is just this paper process transcribed — if you cannot do it by hand, you cannot yet code it.

sections.h: Step 4–5: Brute force first, then hunt the pattern
sections.body:
Write the obvious, slow solution first. A correct brute force proves you understood the problem, gives you a reference to test faster versions against, and in interviews earns most of the marks by itself.

Only then optimise, and optimise by pattern: Does the problem mention pairs or a sorted array? Two pointers. Subarrays with a condition? Sliding window or prefix sums. 'How many times does X occur?' Hashing. Choices that branch? Recursion. With practice these triggers become automatic — that automaticity is what people call 'talent'.

Before declaring victory, try to break it. Feed it 0, 1, negative numbers, a single element, all duplicates, and the maximum size the constraints allow. Programmers think like adversaries of their own code. The Dry Runs and Debugging lesson turns this into a concrete routine.

key_points: Blank-page panic is a process problem: run the checklist instead of waiting for inspiration.
Restate the problem, fix input/output with a concrete example, then decompose into known sub-tasks.
Solve examples by hand first — the repeated steps become your loops and variables.
Always build a correct brute force before optimising; it anchors testing and interviews.
Optimisation is pattern matching: pairs→two pointers, subarrays→sliding window, counting→hashing, branching→recursion.
Finish by attacking your own solution with hostile inputs.

a2z-0004.intro: Before code, there is the plan. A flowchart is a picture of your algorithm — boxes for actions, diamonds for decisions, arrows for flow — and pseudocode is the same plan written as loose, language-free text. Planning in this form forces you to solve the logic while it is still cheap to change, and it is exactly how strong programmers sketch solutions in interviews before writing a single line.

sections.body:
You only need five shapes:

Oval (terminal) — Start and End of the algorithm.
Parallelogram (input/output) — read a value, or display a value.
Rectangle (process) — a calculation or assignment, e.g. sum = sum + n.
Diamond (decision) — a yes/no question; two arrows leave it, one labelled Yes, one No.
Arrow (flow line) — the order in which steps execute.

A loop appears naturally: draw the body in rectangles, then a diamond that asks 'are we done?' with the No arrow looping back up. If you can draw it, you can code it — every flowchart maps one-to-one onto if/else and loop statements.

sections.h: Pseudocode: the same plan in words
sections.body:
Pseudocode keeps the structure but drops the drawing. It uses plain English mixed with programming-shaped lines — INPUT, SET, WHILE, IF...ELSE, PRINT — and indentation instead of arrows. There is no compiler and no strict syntax, so the only thing you can get wrong is the logic itself, which is precisely the point.

Write it at the level where each line will become roughly one line of real code. Too vague ('now process the array') hides the hard part; too detailed (worrying about semicolons) wastes the exercise.

sections.h: Worked example: is a number a palindrome?
sections.body:
Plan it once, use it in every language:

INPUT n
SET original = n, rev = 0
WHILE n > 0:
    digit = n mod 10
    rev = rev * 10 + digit
    n = n div 10
IF rev == original: PRINT 'Palindrome'
ELSE: PRINT 'Not a palindrome'

Trace it with n = 121: digits come off as 1, 2, 1 and rev builds 1 → 12 → 121, equal to the original. Notice the plan already forced the two decisions beginners forget: saving the original before destroying n, and using integer division so the loop terminates.
sections.code:
INPUT n
SET original = n, rev = 0
WHILE n > 0:
    digit = n mod 10
    rev = rev * 10 + digit
    n = n div 10
IF rev == original:
    PRINT "Palindrome"
ELSE:
    PRINT "Not a palindrome"

sections.body:
One Start, one End, and every path through the chart must reach End. Label both arrows leaving a diamond — an unlabelled branch is an unmade decision. Every loop needs an exit condition that the loop body actually moves towards; if the diamond's answer can never change, you have drawn an infinite loop.

The most common beginner mistake is skipping the plan once problems feel 'easy' — then drowning in code when a medium problem arrives. Two minutes of pseudocode routinely saves twenty minutes of debugging.

key_points: Five symbols suffice: oval (start/end), parallelogram (input/output), rectangle (process), diamond (decision), arrows (flow).
A loop is just a decision diamond whose No-branch arrows back to the body — and it must have an exit the body moves towards.
Pseudocode is the same plan in indented words: no syntax to fight, so only logic can be wrong.
Each pseudocode line should become roughly one line of code — vague lines hide the hard part.
Plan first on anything non-trivial: two minutes of pseudocode saves twenty of debugging.

a2z-0005.intro: Knowing flowchart symbols is useless without a method for applying them. This lesson works through the classic beginner problems — reversing a number, GCD, counting digits — the flowchart way: identify input and output, find the repeating step, choose the decision that stops it, then trace with real numbers. These three problems share one skeleton, and recognising skeletons is the whole game in DSA.

sections.h: The four questions that build any flowchart
sections.body:
Ask, in order: (1) What comes in, and what must go out? (2) If I did this by hand, what step would I repeat? That repetition is your loop body. (3) How do I know when to stop repeating? That is your decision diamond. (4) What values must I remember between repetitions? Those are your variables, and they must be initialised before the loop.

Almost every beginner flowchart bug is one of these four questions left unanswered — most often (4), the missing initialisation.

Input: 1234. Output: 4321. By hand you peel digits off the right (4, 3, 2, 1) and build the answer by shifting left and appending: 0 → 4 → 43 → 432 → 4321. The repeated step is 'take last digit (n mod 10), append it (rev = rev * 10 + digit), drop it (n = n div 10)'. Stop when n becomes 0. Variables: rev starts at 0, and a copy of the input is unneeded here because the original is not used afterwards.

The same skeleton with a different 'append' rule solves a family: count digits (increment a counter instead), sum of digits (add the digit instead), largest digit (keep a maximum instead). One loop, four problems — this is why the digit-extraction loop is worth mastering first.

sections.h: Worked problem 2: GCD by Euclid's idea
sections.body:
GCD(48, 18): repeatedly replace the larger number by the remainder of the division — (48, 18) → (18, 12) → (12, 6) → (6, 0) — and the last non-zero value, 6, is the answer. In flowchart terms: a decision 'is b equal to 0?' guards a loop whose body is (a, b) = (b, a mod b).

Trace a second pair on paper before coding: GCD(17, 5) → (5, 2) → (2, 1) → (1, 0) → answer 1. If your trace and your code ever disagree, the trace is right and the code is wrong — that is the entire philosophy of the next lesson.

sections.h: From flowchart to code without tears
sections.body:
Translate mechanically: each rectangle becomes a statement, each diamond becomes an if or a while condition, each loop-back arrow becomes the loop's closing. Then trace the code with the same numbers you used on paper, writing variable values in a small table. If the table matches your hand trace, ship it.

Do not 'improve' the code while translating — optimise later, on a working solution. Most beginner disasters come from editing logic mid-translation and losing track of which version was correct.

key_points: Build any flowchart by answering four questions: inputs/outputs, the repeated step, the stopping decision, the variables to remember.
Digit problems share one skeleton: digit = n % 10, update an accumulator, n = n // 10, stop at 0.
Changing only the accumulator turns that skeleton into count digits, sum of digits, reverse, or largest digit.
Euclid's GCD loop: (a, b) = (b, a % b) until b is 0; trace it on paper before coding it.
Translate flowcharts mechanically, then verify code against your paper trace — never optimise mid-translation.

a2z-0006.intro: Professional programmers do not stare at code hoping to spot the bug — they dry run it. A dry run means executing your own code on paper, one line at a time, tracking every variable in a table. Combined with a habit of testing edge cases first, it turns debugging from panic into a procedure. This lesson gives you that procedure, plus the catalogue of hostile inputs that break beginner programs.

sections.body:
Draw columns for each variable and one row per step. Run the code with a small input and write down every change. Example — summing the digits of 405 with the loop 'while n > 0: s += n % 10; n //= 10':

step | n   | digit | s
start| 405 |   -   | 0
1    | 40  |   5   | 5
2    | 4   |   0   | 5
3    | 0   |   4   | 9

The answer 9 is correct — and notice the trace also proves the loop terminates, because n shrinks every iteration. If a trace column ever stops changing while the loop continues, you have found an infinite loop before the computer did.

Run every solution against this checklist before trusting it:

Zero and one — loops that never run, and formulas that divide by the input.
Negative numbers — digit loops and remainders behave differently; does the problem even allow them?
Empty and single-element inputs — arrays and strings of length 0 and 1 break more solutions than any other case.
All duplicates / already sorted / reverse sorted — inputs with no variety expose hidden assumptions.
The maximum constraint — does the answer overflow a 32-bit integer? Does an O(n^2) loop survive n = 100000?

In interviews, naming the edge cases you tested is itself a strong positive signal.

Step 1: Reproduce. Find the smallest input that fails and keep it — never debug against a huge input. Step 2: Verify understanding. Dry run that input and find the first step where reality departs from your expectation; the bug lives at or before that step, never after it. Step 3: Form one hypothesis ('the loop stops one iteration early') and test only that. Step 4: Fix the root cause, then re-run the failing case and your earlier passing cases.

What not to do: change random lines hoping the answer improves. Every unexplained change destroys information about where the bug was.

sections.h: The five bugs you will meet repeatedly
sections.body: Off-by-one: loop runs one time too few or too many — trace the first and last iteration specifically. Uninitialised accumulator: sum or count starts from garbage instead of 0. Destroyed input: you consumed n in a loop and then needed the original — copy it first. Wrong division: in many languages 5 / 2 is 2, not 2.5 — use integer division deliberately. Condition copied wrong: < instead of <=, which only shows up on boundary inputs — exactly the ones in the edge-case catalogue.

key_points: A dry run is a paper execution: one row per step, one column per variable — it proves correctness and termination.
If a variable stops changing inside a loop, you have an infinite loop; if a trace and code disagree, trust the trace.
Test the catalogue: 0, 1, negatives, empty, single element, all duplicates, sorted/reverse-sorted, maximum size.
Debug by procedure: shrink the failing input, find the first wrong step, test one hypothesis, fix the root cause.
The recurring five: off-by-one, uninitialised accumulator, destroyed input, wrong division, flipped comparison.

a2z-0007.intro: C++, Java or Python? Beginners lose weeks to this question, but the honest answer is simple: for DSA and placements, any of the three works, and depth in one beats shallow knowledge of all. This lesson explains what a programming language actually provides, compares the three realistic choices on the things that matter, and gives you a decision rule so you can stop choosing and start coding.

sections.body: A programming language is three things: a syntax for expressing instructions, a standard library of ready-made tools (sorting, collections, maths functions), and an execution model — compiled ahead of time (C++, Java) for speed, or interpreted line by line (Python) for flexibility. DSA concepts themselves — arrays, recursion, hashing — are identical in all three; only the spelling changes. That is why switching later costs days, not months, but switching repeatedly costs you the depth that interviews reward.

C++ — the placement default in India. Fastest execution, the powerful STL library, and most interview problem sets assume it. Costs: verbose syntax, manual memory awareness, and cryptic error messages while learning.

Java — the enterprise favourite. Slightly slower to write than Python but very structured; strong Collections framework; common in service-company and backend interviews. Costs: boilerplate (everything lives in a class), slower startup.

Python — the fastest to learn and to write. Ideal first language and superb for interviews at product companies that allow it. Costs: slower raw speed (rarely decisive, since complexity class matters more), and some campus drives expect C++/Java.

As a text summary:
Language | Speed of writing | Speed of running | Library for DSA | Campus popularity
C++      | Slow             | Fastest          | STL (excellent) | Highest
Java     | Medium           | Fast             | Collections     | High
Python   | Fastest          | Slowest          | Built-ins+modules | Medium, growing

If your target companies or campus drives are known, match their expectation — that overrides everything. Otherwise: choose C++ if you are placement-focused and willing to climb a steeper first month; choose Python if you are starting from absolute zero and want logic first, syntax later (you can add C++ in a few weeks once concepts click); choose Java if you also aim at backend/Android roles.

Then commit for at least the whole beginner module. The language is a vehicle; DSA is the driving. Nobody ever failed an interview because they picked Java over C++ — they failed because they knew neither deeply.

In your chosen language you should be fluent in: variables and types, conditions and loops, functions, arrays/lists, strings, one hash map and one set type, sorting, and basic recursion — plus fast input/output. That list is exactly what the next three lessons (Learn C++, Learn Java, Learn Python) and the library lessons in this module build. Fluency means writing these without looking them up; everything rarer can be looked up forever.

key_points: A language = syntax + standard library + execution model; DSA concepts are identical across all three.
C++: fastest, STL, campus default, steepest start. Java: structured, Collections, boilerplate-heavy. Python: fastest to write, slowest to run.
Decision rule: match your target companies if known; otherwise C++ for placement focus, Python for a zero-start, Java for backend ambitions.
Depth in one language beats shallow knowledge of three — commit for the whole beginner module.
Fluency target: types, loops, functions, arrays, strings, map/set, sorting, recursion, fast I/O.

a2z-0008.intro: C++ is the default language of competitive programming and Indian campus placements: it runs fast, its STL library hands you sorted structures, heaps and hash maps for free, and most problem sets are tested against it. This lesson is an orientation — the skeleton of every C++ program, fast input/output, the core syntax you need for this sheet, and the road map for what to learn next.

sections.body: Every C++ program starts from the same frame: include the library, use the std namespace, and put your logic in main(). The single header bits/stdc++.h pulls in the entire standard library, which is why competitive programmers never list individual includes. return 0 signals success.

cin and cout are convenient but slow by default because they stay synchronised with C streams. The two lines ios::sync_with_stdio(false) and cin.tie(nullptr) remove that overhead — paste them at the top of main() in every program. End output lines with '\n' rather than endl; endl also flushes the buffer, which is slow inside loops. When input is truly huge, scanf/printf or fast scanning exists, but with fast i/o switched on, cin handles contest-sized input fine.

Types: int (about ±2.1 billion), long long (about ±9.2 × 10^18 — use it whenever an answer might exceed int), double for decimals, char, bool, and string. Conditions and loops look like most C-family languages: if / else if / else, for (init; condition; update), while, and do-while.

Functions declare their return type and parameter types — int gcd(int a, int b). Arrays are fixed-size blocks: int a[100]; and the flexible workhorse is vector<int>, which grows dynamically. Strings support + concatenation and direct comparison. Two C++-specific habits matter from day one: integer division truncates (7 / 2 is 3), and indices are 0-based everywhere.

sections.h: Your C++ road map for this sheet
sections.body: In order: (1) this skeleton plus conditions and loops until pattern problems feel mechanical; (2) functions and recursion; (3) arrays and strings; (4) the STL lesson in this module — vector, pair, map, set, stack, queue, priority_queue and the sort/lower_bound algorithms. Everything else in C++ (classes, pointers in depth, templates) can wait until DSA is well under way. Judge yourself by problems solved, not chapters read.

key_points: One header (bits/stdc++.h) plus using namespace std plus main() is the universal C++ skeleton.
Always enable fast I/O: ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr); and prefer '\n' over endl.
Default to long long for accumulated answers — int overflows near 2.1 billion.
Integer division truncates (7 / 2 == 3); all indexing is 0-based.
Road map: loops → functions/recursion → arrays/strings → STL. Judge progress by problems, not chapters.

a2z-0009.intro: Java is the language of enterprise software and a very common interview choice: everything lives inside classes, the Collections framework is excellent, and the compiler catches many mistakes early. This lesson is an orientation — the class skeleton every program shares, the two ways to read input, the core syntax for this sheet, and what to learn next.

sections.body: A Java program is a class with a main method; the file name must match the public class name. There is no way around this boilerplate, so memorise the frame once and reuse it forever. System.out.println prints a line; System.out.print stays on the same line.

Scanner is simple — nextInt(), nextLong(), next() for a word, nextLine() for a full line — and is fine for learning and small inputs. Its trap: after nextInt(), the newline stays in the buffer, so a following nextLine() returns an empty string; add a throwaway nextLine() call after numeric reads when you mix the two.

For large inputs Scanner is slow, and competitive code switches to BufferedReader with StringTokenizer, parsing numbers manually. Know that the faster route exists; adopt it when a problem actually times out, not before.

Types: int, long (append L to big literals), double, char, boolean, and String — capital S, because String is a class, which is also why you compare strings with .equals(), never ==. Loops and conditions mirror C++ closely, and methods are just functions inside the class — declare helpers static so main can call them directly.

Arrays are objects with a .length; the flexible list is ArrayList<Integer> — note the capitalised wrapper classes (Integer, Long) because collections cannot hold raw primitives. Strings are immutable: building one with += in a loop creates a new string each time, so use StringBuilder when assembling long output or reversed strings.

sections.h: Your Java road map for this sheet
sections.body: In order: (1) the skeleton, loops and methods until patterns feel mechanical; (2) arrays and strings, including StringBuilder; (3) recursion; (4) the Java Collections lesson in this module — ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet, PriorityQueue, Deque and the Collections utility methods. Object-oriented design (inheritance, interfaces) matters for development interviews but can wait until your DSA base is built.

key_points: Java frame: public class matching the file name, static main, import java.util.* — memorise it once.
Scanner is easy but slow and has the leftover-newline trap after nextInt(); BufferedReader is the fast route.
Compare strings with .equals(), never ==; build long strings with StringBuilder, not += in a loop.
Collections need wrapper types (Integer, not int) — ArrayList<Integer> is your default dynamic array.
Road map: loops/methods → arrays/strings → recursion → Collections.

a2z-0010.intro: Python is the fastest language to learn and to write: no boilerplate, no types to declare, and data structures like lists and dicts built into the syntax itself. For DSA it lets you think about the algorithm instead of the spelling. This lesson is an orientation — how a Python program looks, input done right, the core constructs for this sheet, and the road map through the library lessons.

sections.body: A Python file is just statements, executed top to bottom. Indentation is not style — it is the syntax that defines blocks, so keep it consistent (4 spaces). print() outputs, input() reads a line as a string, and int() converts. The whole 'sum of N numbers' program fits in a few lines:
sections.code:
def solve():
    n = int(input())
    total = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        total += int(input())
    print(total)

solve()

sections.body:
input() always returns a string, so convert explicitly. For a line of space-separated numbers, the idiom is nums = list(map(int, input().split())) — split() breaks the line into words, map applies int to each, list collects them. Reading input one line at a time is fine for this sheet; when inputs grow huge, sys.stdin.readline or reading all of sys.stdin at once is the standard speed fix.

Two arithmetic traps to burn in now: / is true division (7 / 2 is 3.5) while // is floor division (7 // 2 is 3) — digit problems want //. And % is the remainder, your digit-extraction tool.

Numbers (int has unlimited size — overflow simply does not exist in Python), strings (immutable, sliceable: s[::-1] reverses), lists (dynamic arrays: append, pop, sort), dicts (hash maps: counting frequencies is a two-liner), and sets (uniqueness and O(1) membership). Loops: for x in range(n) for counting, for item in list for traversal, while cond for condition-driven work. Functions use def, and multiple return values come back as tuples.

One habit matters more than any other in Python: build strings with ''.join(list_of_pieces) instead of += in a loop, and prefer built-in functions (sum, max, sorted) over hand-written loops — they run at C speed.

sections.h: Your Python road map for this sheet
sections.body: In order: (1) this syntax core until patterns and digit problems feel mechanical; (2) recursion; (3) the two Python Libraries lessons in this module — built-ins and math first, then the DSA power tools: collections.Counter, deque, heapq, bisect and itertools. Python's weakness is raw speed, so you will lean on complexity analysis (the Time Complexity lesson) a little more than C++ users do — a fair trade for writing solutions in half the lines.

key_points: Python has no skeleton and no overflow: indentation is syntax, ints are unbounded, input() always returns a string.
The input idiom: list(map(int, input().split())); digit problems need // (floor division) and % (remainder), not /.
Lists, dicts and sets are built into the syntax — frequencies via dict/Set are everyday tools, not library extras.
Build strings with ''.join(...) and prefer built-ins like sum/max/sorted — they run at C speed.
Road map: syntax core → recursion → Python Libraries Parts 1 and 2.

a2z-0011.intro: Pattern problems look trivial and teach more about loops than any other beginner topic: they force you to control two nested loops precisely and to see a picture as numbers. This lesson covers the approach for the easy and medium band — the shapes built from a single rule per row: rectangles, triangles, pyramids, diamonds and the simpler number and letter patterns (roughly Patterns 1–18 of the Patterns subtopic).

sections.body:
Every pattern program in this band follows the same contract:

Rule 1: the outer loop runs once per row — if the picture has n rows, the outer loop runs n times.
Rule 2: the inner loop runs once per column in that row — its count is a function of the row number.
Rule 3: print the symbol inside the inner loop, without a newline.
Rule 4: print exactly one newline after each row.

When a pattern goes wrong, it is almost always one of these four being violated — the newline inside the inner loop is the classic beginner bug. Your entire job reduces to one question: for row i, how many spaces and how many symbols?

Never start coding from the picture. First, tabulate. Take the star pyramid for n = 4:

row i | spaces | stars
0     | 3      | 1
1     | 2      | 3
2     | 1      | 5
3     | 0      | 7

Now find formulas in i: spaces = n - i - 1, stars = 2*i + 1. Those two formulas ARE the program; the loops are clerical work. If the table has no obvious formula, split the row into segments (spaces, symbols, spaces) and tabulate each segment separately — every easy/medium pattern yields to this.
Translating the table directly — one loop prints the spaces, one prints the stars, then a newline. This three-inner-loop shape (spaces, stars, newline) is the template for every centred pattern.
sections.code:
def star_pyramid(n):
    for i in range(n):
        print(' ' * (n - i - 1), end='')
        print('*' * (2 * i + 1))

star_pyramid(4)
#    *
#   ***
#  *****
# *******

sections.body:
Triangles (Patterns 2–6): the inner count is i+1 or n-i — one formula, growing or shrinking. Pyramids and diamonds (7–10): a diamond is a pyramid followed by its inverse, so write both halves or reuse one function twice. Number triangles (3, 4, 13): the printed value changes — per-row counter, per-column counter, or a running counter that survives across rows (Floyd's triangle). Letter triangles (14–16): print chr(ord('A') + j) — letters are just numbers with a costume on.

Medium patterns add one twist: two different segments per row that must be tracked independently. The observation table handles them unchanged — add a column per segment.

key_points: Four rules: outer loop = rows, inner loop = columns as a function of the row, symbols without newline, one newline per row.
Never code from the picture — tabulate spaces/symbols per row and find the formula in i first.
Centred patterns use three segments per row: spaces, symbols, newline; diamonds are pyramid + inverted pyramid.
Number and letter patterns only change what is printed: a counter, chr(ord('A') + j), or a running counter across rows.
When stuck, add a column to the table per segment — every easy/medium pattern decomposes this way.

a2z-0012.intro: Hard patterns (roughly Patterns 19–22 and the trickier mediums) break the single-formula comfort of the easy band: two quantities change at once, shapes mirror each other, borders matter more than interiors, or every cell depends on its distance from the edge. This lesson teaches the four techniques that crack them — composition, mirroring, border conditions and the min-distance formula.

sections.h: Technique 1: Compose from halves you already own
sections.body: Complex silhouettes are almost always two simpler patterns stacked or placed side by side. The butterfly/symmetry shapes are a triangle and its mirror sharing each row; the diamond was pyramid + inverted pyramid. When a shape intimidates you, draw a line where its behaviour changes and solve each region with the observation table separately — hard patterns are medium patterns wearing a seam.

Mirrored segments never need a separate formula: the right half is the left half read backwards. In a row of width w, column j mirrors column w - 1 - j. The number crown pattern shows the idea — ascending numbers, a gap that shrinks by 2 each row, then the same numbers descending. Build each side from its own loop and let the gap be a third segment in your table.
sections.code:
def number_crown(n):
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        left = ''.join(str(x) for x in range(1, i + 1))
        gap = ' ' * (2 * (n - i))
        right = ''.join(str(x) for x in range(i, 0, -1))
        print(left + gap + right)

number_crown(4)
# 1      1
# 12    21
# 123  321
# 12344321

sections.h: Technique 3: Border conditions for hollow shapes
sections.body: Hollow patterns (like the hollow rectangle) print a symbol only on the boundary and spaces inside. The condition is pure index logic: cell (i, j) is on the border when i == 0 or i == n - 1 or j == 0 or j == m - 1. One if inside a plain double loop solves the whole family — hollow triangles, hollow diamonds and frames all reduce to choosing the right border predicate for the shape's geometry.

sections.h: Technique 4: The min-distance formula for concentric patterns
sections.body: The number pattern (Pattern 22) prints, in every cell, a value that depends on how deep the cell sits inside the square. Depth of cell (i, j) in a square of side s is min(i, j, s-1-i, s-1-j) — its distance to the nearest edge — and the printed value is n - depth. No state, no counters: the cell's coordinates alone decide its value. Whenever a pattern looks the same at every scale, suspect a distance formula.
sections.code:
def number_pattern(n):
    s = 2 * n - 1
    for i in range(s):
        row = []
        for j in range(s):
            depth = min(i, j, s - 1 - i, s - 1 - j)
            row.append(str(n - depth))
        print(' '.join(row))

number_pattern(3)
# 3 3 3 3 3
# 3 2 2 2 3
# 3 2 1 2 3
# 3 2 2 2 3
# 3 3 3 3 3

sections.body: Work at n = 3 or 4 and print your formula table beside the output: for each row write the expected segment counts from the picture, then instrument mentally which segment first disagrees. Almost every hard-pattern bug is a single off-by-one in one segment (gap shrinking by 1 instead of 2 is the classic), and comparing segment by segment finds it in one pass instead of ten blind edits.

key_points: Hard patterns are composites: find the seam, solve each region with its own observation table.
Mirror segments need no new formula — column j mirrors column w - 1 - j.
Hollow shapes are one border predicate inside a plain double loop (i/j on an edge).
Concentric patterns are coordinate formulas: value = n - min distance to any edge.
Debug segment by segment at n = 3–4; expect a single off-by-one, most often in the shrinking gap.
