a2z-0035.intro: Time complexity is the skill that separates 'my code works' from 'my code passes'. Instead of timing programs in seconds — which changes with every machine — we count how the number of operations grows with the input size n, and describe that growth with Big-O notation. Master the counting rules here and you will be able to look at any loop or recursion in this sheet and predict, before running it, whether it survives the constraints.

sections.h: Why we count operations, not seconds
sections.body:
A stopwatch lies: the same program runs ten times faster on a new laptop, and a 'fast' algorithm in Python can lose to a 'slow' one in C++ on small inputs. What is stable across machines is the growth pattern — if input doubles, does the work double, quadruple, or explode? Big-O keeps only the dominant term of that growth and drops constants: 3n + 5 is O(n); n^2 + 100n is O(n^2), because for large n the n^2 term swamps everything else.

The growth ladder, slowest-growing first:
O(1) constant — array access, one arithmetic op
O(log n) logarithmic — binary search: n can be astronomically large
O(n) linear — one pass over the data
O(n log n) — good sorting: the practical speed limit for big inputs
O(n^2) quadratic — nested loops over the data: fine to ~10^4, dead by 10^5
O(2^n) exponential — naive recursive Fibonacci: dead by n ≈ 45
O(n!) factorial — all permutations: dead by n ≈ 12

Rule 1 — sequential work adds: a loop of n followed by another loop of n is O(n) + O(n) = O(n), not O(n^2).
Rule 2 — nested work multiplies: a loop of n containing a loop of n is O(n^2); if the inner loop runs only to i (a triangle), the total is n(n+1)/2, still O(n^2).
Rule 3 — halving is logarithmic: any loop that divides the problem size by 2 each step (i //= 2, binary search, Euclid's GCD) runs O(log n) times.

Apply them mechanically: read the code inside-out, multiplying as you exit each nesting level, adding as you pass sequential blocks. Watch inner bounds: a loop 'for j in range(i, n)' depends on i, so estimate its total across all i rather than assuming n every time.
sections.code:
n = 100  # input size
total = 0
for i in range(n):        # n times
    for j in range(n):    # n times each
        total += 1        # -> O(n^2)

x = n
while x > 1:              # halves each step
    x //= 2               # -> O(log n)

sections.h: Recursion: count the calls, then the work per call
sections.body:
For recursion, total time = (number of calls) × (work per call). A function that calls itself once on n-1 (sum of first N, factorial) makes n calls — write the recurrence T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) — and costs O(n). Binary search gives T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n).

The trap is branching recursion: naive Fibonacci calls itself twice, T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1), and the call tree has roughly 2^n nodes — exponential, even though each call is trivial. Drawing the first three levels of the call tree is the fastest way to smell exponential blow-up. Dynamic programming, later in this sheet, exists precisely to collapse such trees.

Space complexity counts memory growth with n. A few scalar variables are O(1) extra space; building a new array of size n is O(n). Recursion charges rent too: each live call holds a stack frame, so a recursion of depth n costs O(n) stack space even if it 'uses no arrays' — the hidden cost beginners forget when converting loops to recursion.

Say 'auxiliary space' when you mean extra space beyond the input itself; interviewers use the distinction to test whether your O(1)-space claim is honest. In-place algorithms (reversing an array by swapping) are the gold standard where achievable.

sections.h: Worst, average, best — and the constraint reflex
sections.body:
Big-O usually quotes the worst case, because guarantees matter. But some structures shine on average: hash lookups are average O(1), worst-case O(n). Mention both when they differ.

Finally, build the reflex that maps constraints to budgets. Roughly 10^8 simple operations run in about a second in C++ (fewer in Python). So: n ≤ 10^5 demands O(n log n) or better; n ≤ 10^3 tolerates O(n^2); n ≤ 20 hints the intended solution is exponential or bitmask-based. Read the constraint before choosing the approach — it is the problem quietly telling you its intended complexity.

Believing O(2n) and O(n) differ — constants are dropped, they are the same class. Forgetting that input reading and output printing themselves cost O(n). Analysing only the happy path of a recursive function and missing the branching factor. And the subtlest: summing loop bounds wrongly — an inner loop that runs to i inside an outer loop to n is still quadratic overall, while two separate sequential loops are merely linear. Draw the loops; count honestly.

key_points: Big-O describes growth: drop constants and lower terms; the dominant term is the whole story.
Loop rules: sequential adds, nested multiplies, halving is O(log n).
Recursion cost = number of calls × work per call; two-branch recursion is usually exponential.
Recursion depth is space too — depth n costs O(n) stack, even with no arrays.
Quote worst case by default; state average separately when it differs (hashing).
Read constraints first: n ≤ 10^5 → O(n log n); n ≤ 10^3 → O(n^2) OK; n ≤ 20 → exponential intended.

a2z-0036.intro: The Standard Template Library is C++'s built-in arsenal: ready-made containers (vector, map, set, stack, queue, priority_queue), iterators that connect them, and algorithms (sort, binary search, accumulate) that work on all of them. Learning the STL is the single highest-leverage step in C++ DSA — most 'hard' implementation work becomes a few library calls, and your effort moves to the actual logic.

sections.h: The mental model: containers, iterators, algorithms
sections.body:
Containers own the data and each has a personality: vector is a growable array, map is a sorted key-value tree, unordered_map is a hash table, set keeps unique sorted values, priority_queue always exposes the largest. Iterators are generalised pointers that walk a container. Algorithms are free functions — sort(v.begin(), v.end()) — that operate on iterator ranges, so one algorithm serves every container.

Everything in the STL has a known complexity, and choosing a container IS choosing your complexities: the table later in this lesson is the part to internalise.

sections.h: vector and pair: the daily drivers
sections.body: vector<T> is your default sequence: push_back appends in amortised O(1), v[i] accesses in O(1), v.size() reports length, and sort + reverse give you the two most used algorithms. pair<T,U> bundles two values (access via .first and .second) and compares lexicographically, which makes vector<pair<int,int>> the standard trick for 'sort by one field, break ties by another'.

sections.h: map vs unordered_map, set vs unordered_set
sections.body:
map (balanced tree) keeps keys sorted and guarantees O(log n) for insert/find/erase; unordered_map (hash table) averages O(1) but has no order and a bad worst case. Rule of thumb: need sorted order, predecessor/successor, or range queries → map; need pure frequency counting or membership at scale → unordered_map. The same choice exists for set/unordered_set when you store keys without values.

Frequency counting is the most common STL pattern in this whole sheet:

stack<T> gives push/pop/top in O(1) — last in, first out; it powers bracket matching and 'previous greater element' problems. queue<T> is first in, first out for BFS-style level processing. priority_queue<T> is a max-heap: top() is the largest element, push/pop cost O(log n); for a min-heap write priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>. 'Top K' problems are almost always a heap of size K — keep the K best, evict the worst.

sort(first, last) and sort with a comparator lambda for custom order (e.g. by second element, or descending). binary_search, lower_bound (first element ≥ x) and upper_bound (first > x) on any sorted range, all O(log n). max_element / min_element return iterators — dereference with *. accumulate sums a range (start it with 0LL to avoid int overflow). reverse, count, find and __gcd(a, b) round out the everyday set.

Complexity summary (text table):
vector access O(1) | push_back O(1) amortised | insert middle O(n)
map / set: O(log n) everything, keys stay sorted
unordered_map / unordered_set: average O(1), no order
priority_queue: top O(1), push/pop O(log n)
sort O(n log n) | binary_search/lower_bound O(log n) on sorted data

Using map where only counting is needed — you pay log factors for order you never use. Forgetting that unordered_map with adversarial keys can degrade (rare in practice, real in contests). Erasing from a vector inside a loop and invalidating iterators — erase returns the next valid iterator; use it. Sorting a vector of pairs expecting stability that is not guaranteed. And the quiet classic: accumulate with an int initial value overflowing silently on large sums.

key_points: STL = containers + iterators + algorithms; picking a container means picking your complexities.
vector is the default sequence; pair compares lexicographically, ideal for tie-broken sorting.
map/set: sorted, guaranteed O(log n). unordered_map/set: average O(1), no order — use for counting and membership.
priority_queue is a max-heap (flip with greater<int>); top-K problems = a heap of size K.
Memorise: sort, lower_bound/upper_bound, binary_search, max_element, accumulate (start with 0LL), __gcd.
Frequency counting with unordered_map is the most reused pattern in the entire sheet.

a2z-0037.intro: The Java Collections Framework is Java's answer to the STL: a unified family of interfaces — List, Set, Queue, Map — with implementations whose names tell you their trade-offs (ArrayList, HashMap, TreeSet, PriorityQueue...). Fluency here is what makes Java solutions as short as C++ ones. This lesson maps the framework, gives the frequency-counting pattern you will reuse constantly, and lists the traps specific to Java.

sections.body:
Four interface families cover nearly everything:

List — ordered, duplicates allowed: ArrayList (your default), LinkedList.
Set — unique elements: HashSet (fast, unordered), TreeSet (sorted), LinkedHashSet (insertion order).
Queue / Deque — FIFO processing and double-ended work: ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue (a heap).
Map — key-value pairs, technically outside Collection but used identically: HashMap (fast), TreeMap (sorted keys), LinkedHashMap (insertion order).

The naming code: 'Hash' = hash table, average O(1), no order; 'Tree' = balanced tree, O(log n), sorted; 'Array' = backed by a resizable array; 'Linked' = node chain. Once you can decode names, you can guess any class's behaviour before reading its docs.

sections.h: ArrayList vs LinkedList — the one real List decision
sections.body:
ArrayList stores elements in a growable array: get(i) is O(1), add at the end is amortised O(1), but inserting or deleting in the middle shifts everything — O(n). LinkedList stores nodes with next/previous links: insertion at a known node is O(1), but reaching that node (get(i)) is O(n).

Verdict for DSA: ArrayList almost always. LinkedList wins only when you repeatedly insert/remove at the head or via an iterator you already hold — and even then ArrayDeque usually beats it for queue work. Declaring variables as the interface (List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();) lets you swap implementations with a one-word change.

HashMap<K,V> gives average O(1) put/get/containsKey. The single most-used pattern in this sheet is frequency counting, and Java's getOrDefault (or merge) makes it a one-liner inside the loop. Keys must implement equals and hashCode properly — built-in types (Integer, String, Character) already do; your own classes must override both, consistently.

sections.h: PriorityQueue, Deque and the Collections toolbox
sections.body:
PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default — peek/poll give the smallest; pass Comparator.reverseOrder() for a max-heap. Poll and offer cost O(log n), peek is O(1). Top-K problems: keep a heap of size K and evict the smallest as you go.

Use ArrayDeque for stacks and queues (push/pop/peek for stack behaviour, offer/poll for queues) — the legacy Stack class is synchronised and slow, and LinkedList-as-queue is rarely better.

The static Collections class supplies the algorithms: sort (O(n log n), stable), reverse, frequency(collection, x), max, min, binarySearch (sorted lists only), and shuffle. Arrays.sort does the same for raw arrays — and for int[] it is a fast dual-pivot quicksort, while object arrays get a stable TimSort.

Text summary:
ArrayList get O(1) | add-end O(1) amortised | insert/delete middle O(n)
HashMap/HashSet average O(1) | TreeMap/TreeSet O(log n), sorted
PriorityQueue peek O(1) | offer/poll O(log n)

Traps: (1) Autoboxing — collections hold Integer, not int; unboxing a null value throws NullPointerException, a classic when a map key is absent. (2) == compares references on objects; use .equals for values — two Integer objects with the same value can fail == outside the small cache range. (3) Removing elements from a list while iterating by index skips elements; use an Iterator or iterate backwards. (4) HashMap order is unspecified — if a test expects sorted output, use TreeMap or sort explicitly.

key_points: Decode class names: Hash = average O(1), unordered; Tree = O(log n), sorted; Array = array-backed; Linked = node chain.
ArrayList is the default List (O(1) get); LinkedList rarely wins in DSA — prefer ArrayDeque for queue/stack work.
Frequency counting: freq.put(x, freq.getOrDefault(x, 0) + 1) — the pattern behind a dozen problems.
PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default; reverseOrder() makes it a max-heap; top-K = heap of size K.
Use .equals, never ==, for object values; guard against null unboxing from absent map keys.
Collections.sort/frequency/max/binarySearch and Arrays.sort cover the standard algorithm needs.

a2z-0038.intro: Python's motto is 'batteries included', and Part 1 covers the batteries you will reach for daily: the built-in functions that replace whole loops (sum, sorted, enumerate, zip), the math module, and the essential methods of lists, dicts, sets and strings. The theme is simple — in Python the built-in is almost always both shorter and faster than the loop you were about to write, because it runs in C underneath.

sections.body:
Learn these until they are reflexes:

sum(iterable), min, max — totals and extremes without an accumulator loop.
sorted(iterable, key=..., reverse=True) — returns a new sorted list; key is a function extracting what to sort by (e.g. key=len, or key=lambda p: p[1]).
enumerate(iterable) — yields (index, value) pairs, ending the awkward range(len(...)) dance.
zip(a, b) — walks two sequences in lockstep; zip(*pairs) unzips.
any / all — short-circuit checks over a condition.
abs, round, pow(base, exp, mod) — pow with a modulus does fast modular exponentiation for free.

Writing these by hand is not wrong, but in an interview the built-in shows fluency — and it removes whole categories of off-by-one bugs.

import math unlocks the standard toolkit: math.gcd(a, b) (Euclid, done for you), math.lcm, math.factorial, math.isqrt(n) — the exact integer square root, essential for prime and divisor loops where float sqrt can round wrongly on huge inputs — math.sqrt for floats, math.ceil / math.floor, math.log2 and math.log10, math.comb(n, r) for combinations, and constants math.pi / math.inf. Prefer math.isqrt over int(math.sqrt(n)) whenever the result must be exact.
sections.code:
import math

print(math.gcd(48, 18))        # 6
print(math.lcm(4, 6))          # 12
print(math.isqrt(50))          # 7  (exact)
print(math.factorial(5))       # 120
print(math.comb(5, 2))         # 10

sections.body:
Lists: append/pop from the end are O(1); insert(0, x) and pop(0) are O(n) because everything shifts — if you need front operations, that is what deque (Part 2) exists for. list.sort() sorts in place; slicing a[::-1] builds a reversed copy; list comprehensions ([x*x for x in nums if x > 0]) are the idiomatic filter-map in one line.

Dicts preserve insertion order and give O(1) average lookup; d.get(key, default) reads safely, d.items() iterates pairs. Sets give O(1) membership (x in s) and one-line uniqueness: len(set(nums)) counts distinct values. The membership test is the quiet superpower — replacing 'x in list' (O(n)) with a set turns many O(n^2) beginner solutions into O(n).

Strings are immutable sequences: s.split() splits on whitespace, sep.join(list) assembles, s.strip() trims ends, s.lower() / s.upper() change case, s.count(sub) and s.find(sub) search, and s.isdigit() / s.isalpha() classify characters. Reversal is s[::-1]; building via ''.join(pieces) beats += in loops.

For input at scale, replace input() with sys.stdin.readline, or read everything once via data = sys.stdin.read().split() and walk an index — the standard Python speed fix on judges.

key_points: Built-ins (sum, sorted with key, enumerate, zip, any/all) are shorter and C-fast — reach for them before loops.
math gives exact tools: gcd, lcm, factorial, comb, and isqrt for precise integer square roots.
List end operations are O(1); front insert/pop are O(n) — that is deque's job (Part 2).
'x in set' is O(1) vs O(n) for lists — converting to a set kills many accidental O(n^2) solutions.
Strings: split/join/strip/find; assemble with ''.join, reverse with [::-1].
Fast input: sys.stdin.readline, or one bulk sys.stdin.read().split().

a2z-0039.intro: Part 2 is the DSA power toolkit: the collections module (Counter, defaultdict, deque), heapq for priority queues, bisect for sorted data, and itertools for combinations and prefix work. These four modules convert whole categories of medium problems into a few lines — frequency questions, top-K questions, sliding windows and sorted-insertion questions all have a dedicated tool here.

sections.body:
Counter is a dict specialised for counting hashable items: Counter(nums) builds the whole frequency table in one call. Its methods do the rest — most_common(k) returns the k most frequent (value, count) pairs, and arithmetic like c1 - c2 discards non-positive counts, which makes anagram comparison a two-liner. Missing keys read as 0 instead of raising.

defaultdict(list) / defaultdict(int) creates values on first access, removing the 'if key not in d' ceremony when grouping items or accumulating counts by hand.
sections.code:
from collections import Counter

freq = Counter([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3])
print(freq.most_common(1))   # [(3, 3)]
print(freq[2])               # 2
print(Counter('aab') == Counter('aba'))  # True -> anagram check

sections.body: A deque (deck) supports O(1) append/pop at BOTH ends — append, appendleft, pop, popleft — where a list pays O(n) at the front. That single fact makes deque the correct tool for queues (BFS level order), sliding-window problems that evict from the left, and monotonic-queue patterns later in this sheet. rotate(k) shifts elements cyclically, a neat trick for rotation problems. If your solution calls pop(0) or insert(0, ...) on a list in a loop, switch it to a deque and the hidden O(n^2) disappears.

sections.h: heapq: priority queues in a list
sections.body: heapq turns a plain list into a min-heap: heapify in O(n), heappush/heappop in O(log n), and heap[0] peeks the smallest in O(1). Python has no max-heap — negate values on the way in and out, or store tuples (-priority, item). Two idioms matter: top-K largest = keep a heap of size K, pushing each item and popping the smallest when the heap exceeds K (the heap then holds exactly the K best); and nlargest(k, iterable) / nsmallest for one-shot answers. Heap entries that are tuples compare element by element — include a tiebreaker (like an index) so Python never tries to compare your payload objects.

sections.h: bisect: binary search on sorted lists
sections.body: bisect works on any sorted list: bisect_left(a, x) is the first index where x could insert keeping order (equivalently, the count of elements < x); bisect_right(a, x) counts elements ≤ x. Their difference is the frequency of x — a complete occurrence counter in O(log n). insort inserts in O(n) because of shifting, so bisect shines for queries, not for building. Whenever you hand-write a binary search for bounds in Python, check whether bisect already says it in one word.

itertools generates iterator building blocks: permutations and combinations (and combinations_with_replacement) for brute-force and backtracking practice; product for Cartesian products (nested loops as data); accumulate for running totals — accumulate(nums) is the prefix-sum array in one call; groupby for collapsing consecutive runs (run-length encoding problems); and chain to iterate several sequences as one. All are lazy generators, so they stream instead of materialising huge lists in memory.

Choosing the tool (text summary):
Counting things -> Counter
Both-ends queue -> deque
Repeatedly need the smallest/largest -> heapq
Queries on sorted data -> bisect
Generate combos/permutations/prefix sums -> itertools

key_points: Counter builds frequency tables in one call; most_common(k) answers most 'top frequency' questions directly.
deque gives O(1) at both ends — any pop(0)/insert(0) loop on a list is an accidental O(n^2) waiting to be fixed.
heapq is a min-heap (negate for max); top-K = a heap capped at size K.
bisect_left/bisect_right on sorted data give insertion points and occurrence counts in O(log n).
itertools.accumulate is prefix sums in one call; permutations/combinations power brute-force practice.
Match the tool to the problem shape: counting→Counter, queue→deque, extremes→heapq, sorted queries→bisect.

a2z-0040.intro: Basic Maths is the first real problem family in the sheet, and it rests on a handful of recipes you will reuse for years: extracting digits with % and //, enumerating divisors up to √n, testing primality, and Euclid's GCD. Every recipe here comes with its complexity and its classic trap. Master this lesson and the entire Basic Maths subtopic (eleven problems) becomes variations on themes you already know.

sections.body:
One loop powers half the family. For any number n: the last digit is n % 10, and removing it is n // 10. Loop while n > 0, updating an accumulator per digit:

Count digits — increment a counter (or use len(str(n)) as a shortcut, but know the loop).
Sum of digits — add the digit.
Reverse — acc = acc * 10 + digit.
Largest digit — keep a running maximum.
Count odd digits — add 1 when digit % 2 == 1.

Two traps: the loop destroys n, so copy it first if the original is needed afterwards (palindrome checks!); and n = 0 never enters the loop — handle it as a special case (0 has one digit, and it is a palindrome). A neat alternative for counting digits of positive n is floor(log10(n)) + 1, but the loop generalises to every other recipe, so learn the loop.
sections.code:
def reverse_number(n):
    rev = 0
    while n > 0:
        rev = rev * 10 + n % 10
        n //= 10
    return rev

print(reverse_number(1234))  # 4321

sections.body:
An Armstrong (narcissistic) number equals the sum of its own digits each raised to the power of the digit count: 153 = 1^3 + 5^3 + 3^3. Algorithm: count digits (k), then run digit extraction accumulating digit ** k, and compare with a saved copy of the original.

A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors (28 = 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14). That recipe belongs to the next section — enumerate divisors in O(√n), sum them excluding n itself, compare. Notice both are 'accumulate a per-piece contribution, compare with the original' — the same shape as the digit recipes, one level up.

Divisors come in pairs: if d divides n, so does n / d, and one of each pair is ≤ √n. So loop d from 1 to √n; whenever n % d == 0, record both d and n // d (once, when they are equal — the perfect-square case). That is O(√n) instead of O(n): for n = 10^12, a million iterations instead of a trillion.

Prime testing uses the same bound: a composite n must have a factor ≤ √n, so trial-divide only up to √n (skip evens after checking 2, for a free 2× speedup). Counting all primes up to N is different: testing each number costs O(N√N), while the Sieve of Eratosthenes — mark multiples of each prime starting from its square — costs about O(N log log N) and is the intended solution.

Euclid's algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), repeating until the remainder is 0 — the last non-zero value wins. It runs in O(log(min(a,b))) steps because the numbers shrink fast; the naive 'try every d from 1 to min' is O(n) and dies on large inputs. LCM then comes free from the identity a × b = gcd(a,b) × lcm(a,b), computed as a // gcd * b — divide before multiplying to dodge overflow in fixed-width languages.

Factorial is the simplest accumulation: result = 1 × 2 × ... × n, O(n) time, and it grows so fast (21! overflows a 64-bit integer) that problems usually ask for it modulo something, or for properties like trailing zeros instead of the value itself.

sections.h: The trap list for this whole family
sections.body: Forgetting to save the original number before a destructive loop. Off-by-one at √n: use d * d <= n, not <, or perfect squares slip through (49 would test as prime-ish in divisor sums). Treating 1 as prime (it is not) and 0/negatives as valid inputs without checking the problem statement. Returning divisors unsorted — the pair enumeration produces them out of order, so sort at the end if the problem asks. And reaching for O(n) loops where the constraint (n up to 10^12) is quietly demanding O(√n).

key_points: One loop, many recipes: digit = n % 10, update accumulator, n //= 10 — count, sum, reverse, largest all share it.
Save the original before destroying n; handle n = 0 explicitly — the loop never runs for it.
Divisors come in pairs around √n: enumerate to √n and record d and n//d (once when equal).
Prime test: trial division to √n only; counting primes to N wants the Sieve, not N separate tests.
Euclid's GCD is O(log) steps; LCM = a // gcd * b — divide before multiplying to avoid overflow.
Factorial explodes fast (21! > 64-bit) — expect modulo or property questions, not raw values.

a2z-0041.intro: The array is the first data structure and still the most important: a contiguous block of memory where every element is reachable in O(1) by index. This lesson covers what that memory picture implies, the traversal patterns that solve most beginner array problems (sum, count, maximum, sortedness), the in-place reversal trick, and the costs that will later motivate fancier structures.

sections.h: The memory picture and why indexing is O(1)
sections.body:
Elements of an array sit side by side in memory, each the same size. The address of element i is base_address + i × element_size — pure arithmetic, no searching — which is why a[i] costs O(1) regardless of the array's size, and why indices start at 0 (the first element is 0 steps from the base).

The same picture explains the weaknesses: inserting or deleting in the middle forces every later element to shift (O(n)), and a fixed-size array cannot grow. Dynamic arrays (Python list, C++ vector, Java ArrayList) hide growth by occasionally copying into a bigger block — amortised O(1) append, the same shifting cost in the middle.

sections.h: Traversal patterns: one pass, one accumulator
sections.body:
Most beginner array problems are a single left-to-right pass with a small accumulator:

Sum — total += x.
Count matching — count += 1 when a condition holds (odd numbers, values above a threshold).
Maximum / minimum — best = max(best, x), seeded with the FIRST element, not 0 (seeding max with 0 fails on all-negative arrays — a classic).
Search — return the index on first match, or a boolean for membership.

Recognising 'one pass, one accumulator' as a shape lets you write these in seconds and save your thinking for problems that genuinely need more.

An array is sorted (non-decreasing) when no element is smaller than its predecessor: scan adjacent pairs and fail on the first a[i] < a[i-1]. Equal neighbours are allowed — non-decreasing vs strictly increasing is a problem-statement detail worth re-reading.

Reversal is the first two-pointer pattern: swap the outermost pair, step both pointers inward, stop when they meet. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space — 'in place' — versus the easy but wasteful build-a-new-array method. This swap-from-both-ends skeleton returns in string reversal, rotation problems and partitioning later.

Index out of range — looping to len(a) inclusive, or touching a[i+1] on the last iteration; adjacent-pair loops must stop one early. Seeding a maximum with 0 instead of a[0] (breaks on all-negative input) and a sum with anything but 0. Modifying a list while iterating over it — removals shift indices under your feet; iterate over a copy or build a new list. Assuming the array is non-empty: a[0] on an empty array is a crash, so decide what empty should return before coding.

key_points: Arrays are contiguous memory: address = base + i × size, so indexing is O(1) and indices start at 0.
Middle insert/delete costs O(n) shifting — that cost is why other structures exist.
Most beginner problems are one pass with one accumulator: sum, count-if, max/min, first-match search.
Seed maximum with the first element, never 0 — all-negative arrays are the trap.
In-place reversal: two pointers swapping inward, O(n) time, O(1) space — a skeleton reused everywhere.
Adjacent-pair loops stop one index early; guard the empty array before touching a[0].

a2z-0042.intro: Hashing is the idea that powers the most useful beginner technique in all of DSA: counting frequencies and answering 'have I seen this?' in O(1). Instead of searching a list linearly for every query, you store values in a structure keyed by the value itself. This lesson builds hashing from a simple frequency array up to the hash map, explains why it is fast on average, and covers the problems this module asks about it.

sections.h: The core idea: trade memory for speed
sections.body:
Suppose you must answer, for many queries, 'how many times does x occur in this array?' Scanning the array per query costs O(n) each. Instead, precompute a frequency table once — one pass, O(n) — and then every query is a single lookup, O(1). That is hashing's bargain: spend memory on a table, buy back time on every lookup.

The simplest table is a frequency array: if values are known to lie in a small range (say 0–100, or lowercase letters), freq[value] += 1 indexes directly by the value. Two lines, no library, unbeatable speed. The hash map of the next section generalises this to any values at all.

sections.h: The hash function and the hash map
sections.body:
A hash map stores keys of any type by running each key through a hash function that converts it to a bucket number. Insert, lookup and delete then touch exactly one bucket — average O(1). When two keys land in the same bucket (a collision), the bucket holds both and the map checks equality within it; well-designed hash functions spread keys so evenly that buckets stay tiny.

The honest complexity statement: average O(1), worst case O(n) if many keys collide — which is why interviews ask 'average or worst?' and why ordered maps (trees, O(log n) guaranteed) exist as the alternative. In Python the hash map is dict; in C++, unordered_map; in Java, HashMap.

sections.h: Character hashing and the anagram connection
sections.body:
For strings over a fixed small alphabet, a plain array beats a map: counts = [0] * 26, and each character c increments counts[ord(c) - ord('a')]. Two strings are anagrams exactly when their count arrays are equal — no sorting needed, O(n) instead of O(n log n). The same trick with a 256-slot array covers all ASCII.

Pattern recognition: any problem phrased as 'same multiset of characters/elements' — anagrams, permutations-in-string, ransom notes — is a frequency-equality problem. Build both tables (or build one and decrement with the other) and compare.

sections.h: Choosing: frequency array, hash map, or set
sections.body:
Frequency array when values are small-range integers or characters and you know the range in advance — fastest and simplest, but impossible for huge or negative ranges without offsetting. Hash map when values are arbitrary (large numbers, strings) or the range is unknown — the general answer. Set when you only need presence, not counts: duplicates removal, 'have I seen this value' (which powers the classic two-sum pattern later), and membership tests inside loops.

One warning: hashing needs the values themselves as keys. If you must count things that are unhashable in your language (lists in Python), convert them first (to tuples) or count a derived key.

Indexing a frequency array with a value outside its range (negative numbers crash it — offset or use a map). Building a frequency table and then scanning the ORIGINAL array to find the max-frequency element when scanning the table is cheaper and cleaner. Forgetting that map iteration order is unspecified in most languages, so tie-breaking ('first element with max frequency') must be handled deliberately, usually by scanning the original array once the max frequency is known. And solving counting problems with nested loops — the O(n^2) smell that hashing exists to eliminate.

key_points: Hashing trades memory for time: build a frequency table once in O(n), answer every lookup in O(1).
Frequency array when the value range is small and known; hash map for arbitrary values; set for presence-only.
Hash map operations are average O(1) (collisions make the worst case O(n)) — state which one you mean.
Anagram-type problems are frequency-equality problems: compare count tables, no sorting needed.
Character counting with a 26-slot array beats a map when the alphabet is fixed.
Tie-breaking on max frequency needs a deliberate rule — map iteration order is not your friend.

a2z-0043.intro: Strings are arrays of characters wearing a friendlier interface — and in Python and Java they are immutable, which changes how you build and modify them. This lesson covers the string mental model, the core operations and their real costs, and the three patterns behind this module's string problems: two-pointer palindrome checking, frequency-based anagram logic, and prefix matching.

sections.h: The mental model: an immutable character array
sections.body:
Indexing, length and iteration behave exactly like arrays: s[i] in O(1), len(s), for ch in s. The difference is immutability in Python/Java (and const-correctness habits in C++): you cannot assign s[0] = 'A'. Every 'modification' builds a new string — which means building a string with += inside a loop copies the whole string each iteration, an accidental O(n^2). The fixes are idiomatic per language: collect pieces in a list and ''.join them (Python), use StringBuilder (Java), or mutate a char array / std::string directly (C++).

Slicing creates copies too — s[::-1] is a beautifully short reversal that costs O(n) memory, fine unless the problem demands in-place work.

sections.h: Core operations and their honest costs
sections.body:
Concatenation of two strings costs O(total length). Searching for a substring (in / find / indexOf) is O(n × m) worst case in naive implementations — fast in practice thanks to optimised library code, but worth knowing. split and join are O(n). Comparing two strings is O(n) in the worst case (they may differ only at the last character), which is why sorting strings costs O(n log n × L), not just O(n log n).

Character arithmetic is the other essential: ord('a') = 97, chr(ord('a') + 3) = 'd'. Case conversion, digit checks (c.isdigit(), Character.isDigit) and alphabet indexing (ord(c) - ord('a') for the 26-slot frequency array) all build on it.

sections.h: Pattern 1: two pointers for palindromes and reversals
sections.body: Place one pointer at each end and walk inward comparing characters: a palindrome survives every comparison until the pointers meet. O(n) time, O(1) extra space, no reversed copy needed. The same skeleton reverses (swap instead of compare) and powers later classics like valid-palindrome-with-skips. Decide the fine print before coding: are comparisons case-sensitive? Do spaces and punctuation count? Problem statements differ, and this decision is where most wrong answers come from.

Frequency logic from the Basic Hashing lesson applies verbatim to characters: anagrams compare count tables, 'sort characters by frequency' sorts the table, 'largest odd number in a string' scans digits with positional awareness. If a string problem mentions counts, your first move is a frequency table.

Prefix problems (longest common prefix and friends) compare position by position across strings: take the first string's character at index i, check every other string has the same character at i, stop at the first mismatch or the end of the shortest string. The shortest string bounds the answer — finding it first is the small optimisation that also prevents index errors.

The += in a loop O(n^2) trap. Comparing strings with == in Java (reference comparison) instead of .equals. Index errors at the boundaries — empty string and single character are the test cases that expose them. Forgetting that sorting-based anagram checks cost O(n log n) when a counting check is O(n). And treating Unicode as single bytes: in most modern languages an index steps over characters/ code points, not raw bytes — know what your language counts.

key_points: Strings are immutable character arrays in Python/Java — build via list + join or StringBuilder, never += in a loop.
Know real costs: concatenation, slicing and comparison are O(n); searching is not free either.
Character arithmetic (ord/chr) unlocks alphabet indexing and case/digit tricks.
Palindromes and reversals are two-pointer problems: compare or swap while walking inward, O(1) extra space.
Counts in a string problem → frequency table first (anagrams, sort-by-frequency).
Prefix problems are bounded by the shortest string — find it first to dodge index errors.

a2z-0072.intro: Recursion is a function that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem, until the problem is so small the answer is immediate. It is the gateway to trees, graphs, backtracking and dynamic programming — and the topic beginners fear most, usually because nobody showed them the call stack. This lesson builds recursion from its two mandatory parts, shows exactly what the computer does while it runs, and gives you a design method that works on every recursive problem in this sheet.

sections.body:
Every correct recursion has:

1. A base case — the smallest input, answered directly with no further call. factorial(0) = 1; sum of an empty list = 0.
2. A recursive case — the answer expressed using the same function on a strictly smaller input: factorial(n) = n × factorial(n - 1).

Two failure modes mirror the two parts: a missing or unreachable base case means the calls never stop (infinite recursion → stack overflow), and a recursive call that does not shrink the input (calling f(n) from f(n)) never reaches the base case. Before anything else, check both, every time.

sections.h: The call stack: what the computer actually does
sections.body:
Each call gets its own stack frame — its own copy of the parameters and local variables — pushed onto the call stack. Trace factorial(3):

factorial(3) waits for factorial(2)
  factorial(2) waits for factorial(1)
    factorial(1) waits for factorial(0)
      factorial(0) returns 1            <- base case
    factorial(1) returns 1 × 1 = 1
  factorial(2) returns 2 × 1 = 2
factorial(3) returns 3 × 2 = 6

The frames pile up on the way down (winding) and resolve on the way back up (unwinding). Nothing is magical: the answer is assembled during unwinding. The stack is also the cost — depth d means d live frames, O(d) space, and a hard limit (Python's default recursion limit is about 1000) beyond which the program crashes.
sections.code:
def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:          # base case
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # recursive case

print(factorial(5))  # 120

sections.h: Reading a recursion as a tree
sections.body:
When a function makes two calls, like naive Fibonacci — fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) — the calls form a tree, and the tree exposes the scandal: fib(3) is computed twice inside fib(5), fib(2) three times, and the tree grows to roughly 2^n nodes. Drawing three levels of the tree is the fastest way to see whether a recursion is linear (one call — a chain, O(n)) or branching (a tree, potentially exponential).

Recognising repeated subproblems in the tree is also the birth of dynamic programming: memoisation stores each subproblem's answer so the tree collapses into a chain. You will meet that properly in the DP module; here, just learn to draw the tree.

sections.h: The design method: define, trust, combine
sections.body:
Write recursions in three steps. (1) Define the contract in one sentence: 'sum_first(n) returns 1 + 2 + ... + n.' (2) Write the base case from the contract: sum_first(0) = 0. (3) Assume — on faith — that the smaller call already fulfils the contract, and write only the combining step: sum_first(n) = n + sum_first(n - 1).

The faith step is the whole trick: you are not supposed to mentally simulate the entire descent while designing. Define the contract precisely, make the input smaller, combine honestly — then verify with a small trace afterwards. Beginners who try to hold the whole stack in their head while writing drown; professionals define and trust.

sections.h: Recursion vs iteration, and the common mistakes
sections.body:
Any recursion can be rewritten as a loop (sometimes with an explicit stack), and loops use O(1) extra space where recursion uses O(depth). Prefer iteration for simple linear scans in production code; prefer recursion when the problem is naturally self-similar (trees, divide and conquer, backtracking) because the recursive form is dramatically clearer.

Mistake list: missing base case; base case that the recursion never reaches (shrinking by 2 from an odd start past a base of exactly 0); doing work with a global variable when a return value was the contract; and assuming recursion is 'slower' — for the same complexity class the difference is a constant factor, while a wrong complexity class (like naive Fibonacci) is the real killer.

key_points: Every recursion = a base case answered directly + a recursive case on a strictly smaller input.
Each call owns a stack frame; answers assemble while the stack unwinds — depth d costs O(d) space.
One recursive call is a chain, O(n); two calls form a tree that can explode to O(2^n) — draw three levels to check.
Design by contract: define what the function returns, write the base case, trust the smaller call, write only the combine step.
Repeated subproblems in the call tree are the signal for memoisation/DP later.
Check the two fatal flaws first: base case missing/unreachable, and an input that never shrinks.

a2z-0073.intro: There are two styles of writing a recursion: return the answer up the stack (functional style), or carry a running answer down through parameters (parameterised style). Real problems — traversing arrays, reversing in place, checking palindromes — usually need parameters that carry position and state, not just a shrinking number. This lesson teaches both styles on the same problem, then the parameter patterns behind this module's recursion exercises.

sections.h: Two styles, one problem: sum of first N
sections.body:
Functional style — the function returns the answer, and each frame combines its own n with the returned smaller answer:

sum_func(n) = n + sum_func(n - 1), with sum_func(0) = 0.

Parameterised style — an extra parameter acc carries the running total down; when n reaches 0, acc IS the answer and is simply returned (or printed):

sum_param(n, acc): if n == 0, return acc; else sum_param(n - 1, acc + n).

Same complexity — O(n) time, O(n) stack — but different thinking: functional style asks 'how do I build the answer from a smaller answer?', parameterised asks 'what state do I need to carry so the base case can finish the job alone?' The second question is the one that unlocks array and string problems.

sections.h: The index parameter: recursing over arrays
sections.body:
Array problems add an index parameter i that walks the structure while the data itself stays put. Sum of array elements: f(i) returns the sum of elements from i to the end; base case i == len(a) returns 0; combine a[i] + f(i + 1). Sortedness check: f(i) compares a[i] and a[i + 1] and ANDs with f(i + 1) — the base case is reaching the last index.

The discipline: the array is never copied or sliced per call (slicing a[i:] copies O(n) data per frame, quietly making your O(n) recursion O(n^2)); only the index moves. This is the single most important parameter habit.

Some problems need a window, not a position: reverse an array in place with f(l, r) — swap a[l] and a[r], then call f(l + 1, r - 1), stopping when l >= r. Palindrome checking is the same window with a comparison instead of a swap. Notice the base case is now a relationship between two parameters, and the state being carried is a shrinking interval — the exact skeleton that later becomes binary search (a window over a sorted array) and divide and conquer.
sections.code:
def reverse_rec(a, l, r):
    if l >= r:
        return
    a[l], a[r] = a[r], a[l]
    reverse_rec(a, l + 1, r - 1)

data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
reverse_rec(data, 0, len(data) - 1)
print(data)  # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

sections.h: What belongs in parameters vs the return value
sections.body:
Rule of thumb: parameters carry what the smaller problem needs to know (position, window, accumulated state, choices made so far); the return value carries what the caller needs back (a sum, a boolean, a count). Boolean searches often short-circuit: if the current check fails, return False immediately without exploring further — recursion respects early exits just like loops.

Carrying 'choices made so far' as a parameter (a current list being built) is exactly backtracking, which the Recursion module later in this sheet develops fully: subsequences, permutations and combinations are all parameterised recursions where the parameter is a partial answer.

Slicing arrays/strings per call (hidden O(n) copy per frame). Mutating a shared accumulator AND returning it, double-counting on the way up. A base case written for one parameter while two are changing (the window recursion that forgets l >= r and only tests l == r walks off the end on even lengths). Default mutable parameters in Python (def f(x, acc=[]) shares one list across calls — use None and initialise inside). And forgetting that parameterised style still pays O(depth) stack: carrying an accumulator does not make Python/C++ tail-call optimise it away.

key_points: Two styles: functional (answer returns up the stack) vs parameterised (answer accumulates in a parameter).
Parameters carry position, window and state; the return value carries what the caller needs back.
Never slice per call — pass an index; slicing copies O(n) per frame and silently makes recursion O(n^2).
Two-parameter windows (l, r) are the skeleton for reversal, palindrome checks and later binary search.
Partial-answer parameters are the bridge to backtracking (subsequences, permutations) in the Recursion module.
Beware mutable default parameters in Python, and base cases that ignore one of two changing parameters.
